procedural_relationships.cited_decision: Hamilton v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2017 BCSC 1334, Kamloops Docket S51613).
procedural_relationships.description: The British Columbia Supreme Court declared title to the four-acre parcel and directed a corrective survey. The Court of Appeal upheld the factual and misdescription conclusions, corrected the limitations reasoning, and dismissed the Crown's appeal.

treatments.cited_decision: Hamilton v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2017 BCSC 1334, Kamloops Docket S51613).
treatments.proposition: The original Crown grant was intended to convey a four-acre parcel containing the hotel and improvements, even though that land straddled subdivisions 7 and 8 and the grant's description placed it in subdivision 8.
treatments.treatment: The Court approved the judge's factual findings as amply supported by the historical and survey evidence and found no basis for appellate interference.

supporting_passages.text:
The Attorney General focused his oral submissions on an argument that there was no evidence to support certain critical findings of fact and the judge had accordingly made palpable and overriding errors of fact. In particular, he contended that there was no evidence that the hotel and other improvements were actually located on LS 7. Rather they were located on LS 8. There was, accordingly, no evidence to support the judge's conclusion that the actual land that was intended to be conveyed included land now known to fall within LS 7.
[14] The Attorney General's submission took respondents' counsel, Mr. Hughes, by surprise. He said that this was a new argument and that it was inconsistent with the Attorney General's position before the judge accepting that the hotel and other improvements were located on LS 7. Mr. Hughes also referred us to a recent survey. This new survey was based on Mr. Ross's field notes from the time he stayed in the hotel in 1901. The "new" survey confirmed that the hotel and improvements were located substantially on LS 7. Although these materials were not before the judge, counsel for the Attorney General conceded that we should have regard to the survey (which he had not previously seen).
He accepted that his submission that the hotel and improvements were on LS 8 was wrong and the judge had not made an error.
[15] It is, in any event, not necessary to rely on this fresh evidence to uphold the judge's findings of fact about the location of the hotel and improvements on LS 7. We were taken to a number of pieces of evidence that amply supported the judge's findings that (a) the hotel and other improvements were located on what is now known to be LS 7, (b) that what was actually conveyed to Cartwright as LS 8 comprised only about 2.4 acres and not the four acres computed by the Crown, and (c) that the four acres intended to be conveyed contained the hotel and improvements. These findings were critical to the judge's conclusion of fact set out in para. 51 referred to above.
[16] The Attorney General argued further that the judge erred in concluding that the Crown intended to grant or convey anything other than what corresponded to the legal description, that is, LS 8, regardless of what Cartwright thought he was going to receive. With respect, I can see no error in the judge's conclusion that the Crown intended to grant the four acres that included the hotel and improvements and that the land it intended to convey was incorrectly described. At the time the grant was made, no complete survey had been conducted, there were no monuments or markings on the land that located exactly where LS 8 lay or the boundary between LS 7 and LS 8, and LS 8 did not yet exist on a survey plan.
The only line that had been properly surveyed, it appears, is the line marking the eastern boundary of section 8, but not LS 8 within it. The survey that had been done by St. Cyr that identified the eastern boundary of section 8 had not been conducted in accordance with instructions. This was the only survey done before the grant. It had to be redone afterwards, and the line marking the eastern boundary of section 8 was resurveyed.
[17] As Mr. Hughes submitted, the Crown grant to Cartwright was ambiguous because it referred to land (LS 8) that had not yet been marked and when it was subsequently marked it proved, as of about 1909, not to match the four acres that the Crown intended to grant (namely the four acres the Crown had computed), but rather it comprised only 2.4 acres.
[18] In my respectful view, the facts found by the judge about what Cartwright applied to acquire and what the Crown intended to grant are amply supported by the evidence. There is no basis for this Court to interfere with them.

quoted_passages.text:
At the time, Carbonite Landing and the surrounding area had not been surveyed. The land was in the railway belt, which, at the time, was owned by Canada pursuant to the Terms of Union, (U.K.), 1871 (34 Vict.), No. 54.
[9] Durick had no legal title to the land, although as a squatter who had made improvements, he may have had priority to buy the land pursuant to An Act Respecting Certain Public Lands in British Columbia, R.S.C. 1886, c. 56, and the Dominion Lands Act, R.S.C. 1886, c. 54. The sale contract therefore does not have any legal effect on the present case; its significance is factual.
[11] In 1897, the Dominion Surveyor General, Edouard de Ville, directed Arthur St. Cyr to subdivide the Columbia River area above Golden into sections. The written direction noted that it would be necessary to traverse the river for the purposes of calculating the area of each quarter section and that it was likely that St. Cyr would have difficulties in marking corners. He was told, "Whatever you do you must provide permanent marks for your lines".
[12] In March 1897 St. Cyr sent de Ville sketches of what he had done to date, including Township 25, the area in which Carbonite Landing was located. Based on those sketches the dominion land surveyor certified the plan for Township 25. We have the plan, but not the sketches, although it is conceivable they are the same.

In 1901, Dominion records note that St. Cyr had not done the survey as directed:
Traversed by St. Cyr in 1897 but not sufficiently to give full areas.
Complete new traverse, together with some section lines, might be made.
[21] In March 1901, the Dominion Surveyor General requested that Mr. Ross, the Dominion land surveyor in Kamloops, re-survey the area. Ross stayed at the hotel at Carbonite Landing on January 31, 1903, as noted in his journal. The Ross survey identified the east boundary of LS 7 a short distance west of the Columbia, and the fact that some of the buildings were on LS 7.
[22] In 1903, Cartwright registered his 1899 grant in the land registry. The certificate of title mirrors the description in the grant and again noted the size as being four acres.
[23] In 1904 Cartwright attempted to get a free grant of part of LS 7 in 1904. The documents noted that the portion he was seeking to acquire had his improvements on it. The Dominion authorities were prepared, as of February 19, 1904, to sell "at the current rate and on the usual terms" if the land was surveyed.
[24] Cartwright engaged James Brady as a private surveyor. Brady's plans confirmed the buildings were west of the line between LS 8 and LS 7 (i.e., on LS 7) and showed the buildings below the natural boundary, on the foreshore of the Columbia, which was provincial land. The Dominion Surveyor General rejected the plan and told Brady to survey again at Cartwright's expense, giving him precise instructions. The Dominion Department of the Interior also said that if the buildings were on the foreshore, Cartwright should ask the province for a grant. The second survey was never done and the sale was never completed. A July 28, 1917 letter from Department of the Interior to the Dominion land agent in Revelstoke noted:
This survey was not satisfactory and no further action was taken in connection with the sale. It would appear, however, that Mr. Cartwright has secured some form of title for the above-mentioned land, probably from the province.
[25] In 1917 the Department of Interior office in Ottawa requested an inspection of improvements made by Cartwright. There is no document showing the purpose of the inspection. On October 2, 1917, a report was forwarded by the land agent in Revelstoke noting that there were improvements on LS 7. It noted that the Registrar of Titles at Nelson could not locate any registrations affecting LS 7, but that four acres in LS 8 was registered pursuant to the 1899 grant.
[26] LS 8 was sold by Cartwright in 1925. The Form A under the Land Registry Act described the land as being four acres. The legal description was that the parcel lay to the west of the Columbia River. The land was transferred five more times before being purchased by the petitioners in November, 1997.
[28] In December 1997 the petitioners had the land surveyed. The survey disclosed that the LS 8 parcel was only 2.4 acres. Much of what the petitioners had been shown was on LS 7, including the unfinished log home and a portion of the cleared area.
[29] The portion of LS 7 on which the buildings are located together with the portion of LS 8 west of the Columbia have been taxed as one parcel.
[30] LS 7 has never been surveyed.
[12] I now set out the critical part of the judgment as it relates to the judge's findings of fact:
[45] The next issue to consider is what was meant to be conveyed in the 1899 grant.
[46] The following are the facts and inferences to be drawn from the documents and events outlined above:
a) In 1893 Cartwright bought the Carbonite Hotel from Durick. The hotel was located on the west bank of the Columbia River. He also obtained possession from Durick of a 40-acre parcel surrounding the hotel on which the hotel was located.
b) From the correspondence and the background facts, the only inference to be drawn is that Cartwright intended to buy the land on which the hotel and its ancillary buildings were located.
c) On that basis, in 1898 Cartwright sought to purchase a five-acre parcel in LS 8. The sale of a four-acre parcel was approved and granted. The only inference to be drawn is that the parcel contained the hotel. While it is not known how much he paid for the land, it was sold and not granted for free.
d) The reason for the change from the five acres requested and the four acres approved in the April 8, 1899 letter must have been that that the Crown looked at the land itself or documents and "computed" (to use the word in the letter) the smaller size.
e) By 1901 it became apparent that the St. Cyr survey was deficient. It was re-done by Ross. The new survey placed the hotel and part of the four-acre parcel in LS 7. Until then it was assumed that the hotel was on LS 8.
f) In order to correct what happened, Cartwright attempted to get the Crown to grant the LS 7 portion of the land he had bought transferred to him for free. The Crown was willing to sell upon a survey being done. A sale never took place.
[47] In short, the Crown and Cartwright thought that the hotel and all the lands purchased in 1899 were situated in LS 8, which had not been surveyed. When a survey was done it revealed that the hotel and some of the land was in LS 7. In other words, what was meant to be conveyed was the four-acre parcel west of the Columbia, which now straddles LS 7 and LS 8.
[48] The Crown argues that what Cartwright bought was what was, in effect, the legal description. There are two problems with that submission. First, it contradicts the law set out above.
[49] Second, there are two parts of the legal description in the grant that - in face of the later Ross survey - contradict one another: a four-acre size and that all four acres are within LS 8. I do not accept that Cartwright was willing to buy whatever the legal description might eventually represent on the ground: he wanted the hotel he was running. I also cannot accept that primacy should be given to the LS 7 part of the description over the four-acre part of the description. As outlined above, the ambiguity must be construed against the Crown.
[51] The original Crown grant intended to convey and did convey a four-acre parcel straddling what is now LS 7 and LS 8 containing what was known as Carbonite Landing and the hotel buildings.
[52] Whether the error in the description or mistaken assumption arose from a survey error by St. Cyr with respect to section lines or from the fact that the legal subdivision had not been surveyed does not matter.

treatments.cited_decision: Hamilton v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2017 BCSC 1334, Kamloops Docket S51613).
treatments.proposition: The grant misdescribed the parcel because the parties intended the four acres containing the hotel while the legal description inaccurately located all of it within subdivision 8.
treatments.treatment: The Court approved the judge's characterization of the error as a correctable misdescription rather than a request to convey land never intended to be granted.

I can see no error in the judge's conclusion that the Crown intended to grant the four acres that included the hotel and improvements and that the land it intended to convey was incorrectly described. [19] It follows from this that the judge did not err in defining the issue as whether a mistake was made in the title of the land conveyed. He concluded that a mistake was made. The legal description misdescribed the land granted and the mistake should be corrected.

treatments.cited_decision: Hamilton v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2017 BCSC 1334, Kamloops Docket S51613).
treatments.proposition: The 2012 Limitation Act governed the pre-existing title claim and exempted it under sections 30 and 3.
treatments.treatment: The Court declined to follow that reasoning because the former 1996 Act governed when the petitioners discovered the claim.

supporting_passages.text:
The judge's reasoning is succinct. He said:
[38] Section 2(1) of the current Limitation Act, S.B.C. 2012, c. 13, provides:
This Act does not apply to the following court proceedings and has no impact on when or if such court proceedings may be brought:
(d) a court proceeding in which the only relief sought is to obtain a declaration;
[39] Section 3(1) of the Limitation Act provides:
3(1) This Act does not apply to the following: ...
(h) a claim for the title to property by any person in possession of that property;
[40] Section 30 of the Act deals with "pre-existing claims". It provides that pre-existing claims with respect to actions referred to in s. 3 are to be dealt with under the current Act.
[41] Even if the relief is not considered to be limited to a declaration, it appears to me that s. 30 and s. 3 are determinative of the limitation issue: the petitioners are in possession of the disputed land and they claim title to it.
[22] The respondents concede that the judge erred in relying on the current Limitation Act

treatments.cited_decision: Hamilton v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2017 BCSC 1334, Kamloops Docket S51613).
treatments.proposition: A possessor's proceeding for a declaration of title was not subject to a limitation period.
treatments.treatment: Although it corrected the governing statute, the Court approved the no-limitation result under section 3(4)(j) of the former Act and dismissed the appeal.

supporting_passages.text:
their claim is not about rectification of a contract. It is a claim seeking a declaration as to title arising from a judicial investigation of title under the Land Title Inquiry Act. That Act does not contain a limitation period. The applicable limitation period is found in s. 3(4) of the former c. 1996 Act, which was in force at the time the petitioners discovered their claim:
(4) The following actions are not governed by a limitation period
and may be brought at any time:
...
(j) for the title to property or for a declaration about the title to
property by any person in possession of that property;
[23] I agree that the respondents' claim is not barred by operation of a limitation period.
[24] In the result, I would dismiss the appeal.

treatments.cited_decision: Hawkes Estate v. Silver Campsites Ltd. (1991), 55 B.C.L.R (2d) 145 (C.A.), applies to this case:
treatments.proposition: Misdescription occurs when an instrument intended to describe one parcel instead describes another or improperly includes adjoining land; it is not merely a correct description of land the applicant does not own.
treatments.treatment: The Court followed Hawkes Estate's definition and applied it to the grant that was meant to describe the hotel parcel but instead located the acreage entirely within subdivision 8.

supporting_passages.text:
the definition of misdescription referred to in Hawkes Estate v. Silver Campsites Ltd. (1991), 55 B.C.L.R (2d) 145 (C.A.), applies to this case:
[72] There are a number of examples of misdescription given in the cases: they have been recited by Gibbs J.A. In my opinion what we have here is not a misdescription. In Turta [Canadian Pacific Railway v. Turta, [1954] S.C.R. 427 ] Cartwright J., in dissent, referred to the case of Hamilton v. Iredale (1903), 3 S.R. (N.S.W.) 535. Walker J. in the Court of Appeal gave, I think, the classic discussion of "misdescription" [pp. 550-51]:
As I understand it the law is to this effect. If I apply to bring Blackacre (to which I am entitled) under the Act, and in my application, or in the certificate, Blackacre is misdescribed so that a certificate is issued to me of the adjoining Whiteacre, or of Blackacre plus a strip of Whiteacre, there is plainly a misdescription of parcels or boundaries, which can be rectified as against me or any volunteer claiming under me. If, however, I apply to have land to which, in fact, I have no title, brought under the Act, and a certificate is issued to me of that land, it is not a case of misdescription of parcels or boundaries. Misdescription is where, intending to describe A, I describe B, or so describe A as to make it include B;
but it is no misdescription if I describe correctly the land I am applying for, though the land is not mine.

treatments.cited_decision: Hamilton v. Iredale (1903), 3 S.R. (N.S.W.) 535. Walker J. in the Court of Appeal gave, I think, the classic discussion of "misdescription" [pp. 550-51]:
treatments.proposition: An instrument misdescribes land when it intends to describe one parcel but describes another or includes part of another; it does not misdescribe land merely because it accurately describes land the applicant does not own.
treatments.treatment: Harris J.A. applied this formulation of misdescription, reproduced through Hawkes Estate, to the grant intended to convey the hotel parcel but legally locating acreage within LS 8.

supporting_passages.text:
Madam Justice Levine's conclusion with respect to the past loss of earning capacity suffered by M.B. for which the Crown was liable is set out at paras. 313-14 of her reasons:
The plaintiff has earned very little in the period from 1987 through 1998. Her tax returns indicate T4 earnings of $6,489, unemployment insurance of $3,750 and workers' compensation of $7,421. She received income assistance from the province of $122,320.96 between September 1991 and November 1998. There is no question that the sexual assault by [the foster father] caused the plaintiff loss of earning capacity up to the date of trial. Taking into account the plaintiff's personal characteristics, all of the contingencies associated with earning income, and the required deduction from any award of the amount of income assistance received (see M.(M.) v. F.(F.)) at p. 183, I assess her damages from that past loss at $10,000.
[9] The latter paragraph contains the only reference in the judgment to deductibility of social assistance benefits. This is not surprising as Madam Justice Levine was bound by the decision of this Court in M.(M.), supra.

there is nothing in the GAIN Act or Regulations which supports the proposition that social assistance benefits were a form of wage replacement or were intended to be compensatory. The benefits provided took the form of both money and services. The essential qualification for obtaining benefits was need. "Income assistance" was defined as meaning assistance through money and services "that is necessary for the purpose of relieving poverty, neglect or suffering." Past employment was not a requirement for benefits and some who received benefits, including persons with physical and mental disabilities, were permanently unemployable. The benefits were not stated to be a form of wage replacement but simply "income assistance".
[59] To the extent that the Legislature turned its mind to ensuring that recipients were not overpaid, it did so in limited circumstances. If overpayment occurred because of fraud, error or other cause going to the initial entitlement to benefits, then benefits must be repaid. If a person had a right to maintenance payments, then the Crown could seek an assignment of those benefits to ensure that the qualifying recipient was paid, but not overpaid.
[60] Does an analysis of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act or Regulations lead to a different conclusion? In my view, it does not. The two pieces of legislation are similar in purpose and intent, although the latter Act may be viewed as placing more emphasis on programs leading to self-sufficiency than the former. A similar conclusion was reached by Madam Justice Baker in Grace v. British Columbia (Lieutenant-Governor in Council), [2000] B.C.J. No. 1201 (B.C.S.C.) (Q.L.), as reflected by the following passages at paras. 80 and 82 of that decision:
I do not agree that the intent of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act is fundamentally different from the intent of its predecessor [the GAIN Act]. . . . The present (Income Assistance) Act may place more emphasis on the relief of poverty through assisting individuals to become self-sufficient, but the purpose of the legislation remains the same - the provision of income support and social services to residents of British Columbia who are in need and the relief of poverty, neglect and suffering in a financially accountable and administratively efficient manner within the limits of the budget set for the Ministry from time to time.
[61] Mr. Justice Donald reviewed the provisions of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act in M.(M.). I do not find it useful to repeat his analysis in that regard. In essence, the range of benefits provided under the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act to individuals and families include the same types of benefits provided under the GAIN Act and Regulations.
[62] Mr. Justice Donald's conclusions with respect to the nature and purpose of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act are set forth at para. 45 of these reasons. In coming to those conclusions, he was considering the receipt of these benefits within the context of the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. While I am considering a different question, namely, whether the receipt of these benefits results in double recovery, I agree with his conclusions with respect to the nature and purpose of the Act.
[63] In my view, a reasonable conclusion one can draw from Mr. Justice Donald's analysis in M.(M.), and from the Acts and Regulations pursuant to which these benefits were paid, is that social assistance benefits do not give rise to double recovery because they are not in the nature of wage replacement. Entitlement to the benefits payable under either the GAIN Act or the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act is in no way related to, or dependant upon, the claimant having suffered a loss caused by a tort. Payment of social assistance benefits is not synonymous with, or even roughly correlative to, payments for past wage loss.
To view them in that way is simply to impose a tort-damages analysis on payments which were not designed to, and do not, duplicate payments by tortfeasors to victims of torts.
[64] Applicants for social assistance benefits may well be victims of torts and their need may be related to the fact that a tort has been committed against them. But the Acts pursuant to which these benefits were paid do not purport to deal with, or contemplate, repayment of benefits from the proceeds of tort awards. Nor do they provide for an assignment of any portion of a tort award for damages. In that regard, it is interesting to note that the B.C. Benefits Manual relating to the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act, provides (under the heading "Policy") that "Assignment or repayment agreements are NOT to be completed for recipients pending ICBC settlements." No reason for this policy is provided, nor were counsel able to assist in that regard.
[65] If the Legislature had intended to do away with a tort victim's rights to collateral benefits, it could readily have done so in a variety of ways. The issue of double recovery in tort has been around for a long time. The Legislature must be taken to be aware of the issue. Decisions such as Parry v. Cleaver, Boarelli and Cunningham have emphasized that, if the retention of benefits in addition to damage awards gives rise to a significant problem, the Legislature is in the best position to weigh the competing social interests and intervene.
Providing rights of subrogation to the payor, an assignment of benefits by a payee, or the imposition of a trust in favour of the payor of benefits provided to the payee are possible alternatives for dealing with this issue if legislation is considered appropriate.
[66] In the result, I am not persuaded that the benefits received by M.B. under either the GAIN Act or the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act duplicate the damage award she received for past loss of earning capacity. When one looks at the nature and purpose of these statutes, it is apparent that the benefits paid pursuant to them constitute income assistance, but not wage replacement. They were paid to her for the same reason they are paid to any recipient, "for the purpose of relieving poverty, neglect or suffering." They were payable as a matter of statutory entitlement independent of any right she may have had to recover damages for loss of income earning capacity arising from tort.
[67] I would add that, even if the social assistance benefits M.B. received could be viewed as a form of wage replacement, difficult questions would arise as to the value of those benefits and the apportionment of their deductibility between tortfeasors (in this case, M.B.'s father and her foster father). Given the conclusion I have reached that these benefits are not properly viewed as wage replacement, it is not necessary for me to examine those questions.
[68] Before leaving this issue, however, I would note that no one has suggested that the value of the social assistance benefits received by M.B. should be set off against any head of damage other than that for past wage loss, or that there should be an overall set-off of the benefits she received against the total amount of damages awarded. In that regard, I note the following comments made by the Ontario Law Reform Commission in its Report on Compensation For Personal Injuries and Death (Toronto: Ministry of the Attorney General, 1987) at pp. 190-1:
Before proceeding to our reform proposals, one important point should be clarified. We believe that the current no-deduction rule can be criticized only insofar as it allows for double recovery with respect to the same pecuniary loss. In our view, a collateral benefit, whether in the nature of insurance or a benevolent payment, that is not clearly duplicative of an item of damage or loss claimed by the injured person from the wrongdoer, cannot be said to constitute double recovery. A non-indemnity accident benefit that pays a specified sum upon proof of the event of an accident, but without proof of loss, cannot be regarded as duplicating recovery for a loss.
Similarly, a gift to an injured person from a relative of a sum of money, not designated to relieve a particular loss, would not be in pari materia with any specific pecuniary claim by the injured person and, accordingly, in our view, cannot be considered, in theory or in fact, double recovery. [Emphasis added.]
[69] Since I have concluded that the social assistance benefits received by M.B. do not represent wage replacement, it cannot be said that M.B. obtained double recovery. On that basis I would affirm the award of $50,000 for past loss of earning capacity, without deductibility of the social assistance benefits

treatments.proposition: The trial order calculated prejudgment interest as if the entire past earning-capacity loss arose on the date of the assault.
treatments.treatment: Prowse J.A. held instead that interest must accrue on a notional stream of income in six-month increments, joining Mackenzie J.A.'s treatment of this issue.

supporting_passages.text: Counsel agreed, however, that interest should be calculated on the award of $10,000 as special damages based on the entire loss having been suffered at the time of the sexual assault. This resulted in an interest award in the amount of $18,551.25.

I agree with Mr. Justice Mackenzie that interest on the award for past loss should be calculated as special damages in accordance with s. 1(2) of the Court Order Interest Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 79, by treating the award as a stream of income received evenly over the period of time starting six months after the cause of action arose (January 1, 1977) and ending at the date of judgment as proposed by the Crown. I would allow the appeal with respect to this issue.

treatments.cited_decision: The judgment of Levine J. is reported at 2000 BCSC 735.
treatments.proposition: The trial judge treated the pretrial earning-capacity award as replacing an income stream and deducted income assistance on the factual premise that M.B. would not have received it while employed.
treatments.treatment: Smith J.A. approved that substance, treating the label 'earning capacity' as terminological and concluding that the payments had already offset part of the proved income loss.

supporting_passages.text:
The relevant pre-trial damage alleged by the plaintiff in her statement of claim in this case was "a loss of income." Although, the trial judge characterized the claim as one for "loss of earning capacity", it is my view that the effect of her award was to replace a lost income stream. The trial judge implicitly recognized this as the essence of the award when she based it upon statistical evidence of average employment earnings of females resident in British Columbia (see her reasons at [2000] B.C.J. No. 909 (Q.L.), para. 310). Moreover, this view is consistent with fundamental principle. The measure of damages is the plaintiff's actual financial loss, not the theoretical value of an untapped abstract capacity to earn.
In my view, the difference in phraseology in respect of pre-trial loss between "loss of income" and "loss of earning capacity" is terminological, not substantive.

the award of damages for pre-trial loss of income in this case has converted a past uncertainty into a certainty - but for her tortiously-caused injuries, the plaintiff would have been employed during the pre-trial period and would have earned income from her employment.
[157] The corollary of this conclusion is that the plaintiff would not have received income assistance benefits while she was working. It is implicit in the deduction of the income assistance payments by the trial judge that, as a matter of fact, the plaintiff would not have been eligible to receive them while she was gainfully employed. It follows that the income assistance payments that the plaintiff received had the effect of partially replacing her lost employment income.
[158] Thus, on the application of fundamental principles, the result is that the plaintiff's past loss of income was offset pro tanto by receipt of the income assistance payments and, to that extent, that she has suffered no loss.

treatments.cited_decision: The judgment of Levine J. is reported at 2000 BCSC 735.
treatments.proposition: The trial judge deducted all income assistance from the assessed past earning-capacity loss as compensation for the same loss.
treatments.treatment: Mackenzie J.A. rejected that deduction because the assistance responded to need in different periods and did not compensate the same loss caused by the two torts.

supporting_passages.text:
Social welfare benefits are "income assistance" under the Act. Income assistance is defined as "a support and shelter allowance". Support and shelter connote need. They are independent of any loss. The trial judge assessed the loss of earning capacity caused by the assaults of the foster father and the biological father together at $10,000, after deducting income assistance of $122,320.96. This Court substituted $50,000 before income assistance reflecting a division between the separate torts of the foster father and the biological father. That loss is spread over the period of 20 years from 1979 when the plaintiff reached age 18 to the trial date in 1999. The income assistance of $122,320.96 was all received between September 1991 and November 1998.
The result of the trial judge's approach is that income assistance received in the 1991 to 1998 period is deducted, in part, from compensation for loss of earning capacity in the 1979 to 1990 period.
[105] I do not think that there is any authority for the proposition that social assistance benefits received in one period can be deducted from damages for loss of earnings suffered in a different period. Clearly it cannot be said to be compensation for the same loss. Factually, this case illustrates the issues of allocation that will arise from deductibility. Apart from the timing difficulties, there is the further problem noted by Prowse J.A. of dividing the benefits between the damages for the tort of the biological father, a claim that has been settled, and the tort of the foster father at issue here. I do not think there is any difference in principle between tortfeasors in terms of deductibility when each tort has contributed to the earnings loss.
[106] While these complications are specific to the present case, they illustrate the difficulties facing deductibility of social assistance benefits more generally. They underline the general proposition that damages and social assistance reflect different compensation objectives and there is no direct connection between them. In my opinion, they are not compensation for the same loss as the issue was framed in Ratych and consequently they do not pass the threshold requirement of double compensation. In my respectful view, the majority opinion in M.(M.) assumed double compensation and in that respect misapplied Ratych.
[107] If there is no double compensation for the same loss, the issues that have engaged the courts since Bradburn in defining the insurance indemnity and charitable benefits exceptions do not arise. This is not a case of indemnity analogous to insurance because the benefits do not indemnify against the same loss caused by the tort. Nor are the benefits charity, the other classic head of non-deductibility going back to Bradburn. In one sense, social assistance benefits are analogous to charity because they involve the relief of poverty. But the analogy ends there. Social assistance benefits are not gratuitous; they are paid by statutory obligation. The statute reflects a broader sense of social obligation than simple charity.
That obligation is expressed in Article 25(1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, U.N. Doc. A/810 (1948), in these terms:
ARTICLE 25(1) Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and his family, including food, clothing, housing, and medical care and necessary social services, and the right to security in the event of unemployment, sickness, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood in circumstances beyond his control. [108] The Universal Declaration is of course only a declaration, without the legal force of an international convention or treaty. Canada has acceded to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights 1966, U.N. Doc. A/6316 (1966), and Articles 9 and 11 of that Covenant may have converted the rights declared in Article 25 into obligations.
The relationship and status in Canada of the Declaration and the Covenant are discussed by Dickson C.J. in Re Public Service Employee Relations Act, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 313 at350-2. Consistent with the Declaration and the Covenant, the BC Benefits Act can be taken as a recognition by the Legislature of a general obligation to relieve poverty and the right of those in need to receive adequate support for their health and well being.
[109] In summary I do not think that the Bradburn categories of collateral benefits are at issue in this case because it cannot be said that the social assistance benefits were paid for the same loss as the tort. They are not an indemnity against a specific loss of income. Nor are they charity, because of the statutory right of the recipient to payment and the implied general obligation. But the threshold test, affirmed in Ratych, is that a deductible benefit must be paid for the same loss. Social assistance benefits are identified with need: they are not an indemnity for the loss claimed in the action. In my view, the threshold test has not been met and the benefits paid to the plaintiff are not deductible.

supporting_passages.text:
At trial, the parties were agreed that the respondent had, prior to the time of trial, received social assistance, or statutory income assistance payments, from the defendant Province in the amount of approximately $122,000. The majority of the payments were paid under the Guaranteed Available Income for Need Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 158, (the "GAIN Act"). This statute was replaced in 1996 with the British Columbia Benefits (Income Assistance) Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 27. The provisions of both statutes are generally similar. In my view, the respective statutes and their associated regulations are meant to provide income assistance for those who are unable to earn an income adequate to support themselves and their dependants.
Such assistance does not, in my opinion, fall under any exception to the general rule against double compensation.
[128] In the Statement of Claim filed in this action in 1997, the plaintiff respondent pleaded that she had suffered a past loss of income and the loss of an ability to earn income in the future. At para. 276 of her 3 May 2000 Reasons for Judgment, Levine J., (as she then was), accepted the evidence of a psychologist that the psychological injuries that the plaintiff had suffered as a result of the activities of her abusers (natural parent and foster parent), made it difficult for the her "to initiate and sustain educational and vocational efforts." At para. 314, the trial judge stated as follows:
There is no question that the sexual assault by J.P. caused the plaintiff loss of earning capacity up to the date of trial.
[129] Although the trial judge did not set out in detail by what methodology she assessed the sum of $132,000 as compensation for past loss of income, or earning capacity, she must have found the loss proven in that amount because, after deducting the amount of social assistance paid in the sum of $122,000, the trial judge assessed damages under this head at $10,000.
[130] The case was appealed to this Court. In its original judgment, handed down 27 March 2001, this Court found that the trial judge had erred in failing to apportion damages between the natural parent and the foster parent in order to reflect the respective amounts of harm caused to the respondent by each parent. The majority found the defendant Province liable for the wrongs committed by the foster parent. Mackenzie J.A. said this at para. 106 of his Reasons:
The trial judge assessed the plaintiff's loss of past opportunity to earn income at $132,320.96, calculated as the amount of income assistance from the province repayable out of any award, plus $10,000. The trial judge's award under this head reflects the same error in failing to allocate the loss between the plaintiff's original position as a result of the prior tort and the loss attributable to the foster father's tort. Adjusting for that error I would vary the award to $50,000, before deduction for income assistance. In my respectful view, the income assistance arrangement is a collateral matter between the plaintiff and the provincial government that should not influence the quantum of the tort award.
[131] As noted in the Reasons of Prowse J.A., it became apparent after the delivery of the judgment that it would be necessary to reconsider both the issue of deductibility of social assistance payments and the method of interest calculation on the past loss award.

In this case, the respondent argues that we should overrule the following conclusions expressed by Esson J.A., speaking for the majority, in the case of M.(M.) v. F.(R.) (1999), 52 B.C.L.R. (3d) 127 (C.A.) at pp. 181-82:
The final question is that as to the deductibility of welfare benefits. The Ontario Court of Appeal, in Boarelli v. Flannigan (1973), 36 D.L.R. (3d) 4 (Ont. C.A.) held that such benefits are not to be deducted. I agree with the learned trial judge that the reasoning upon which that decision was based was overruled by the Supreme Court of Canada in Ratych v. Bloomer, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 940 (S.C.C.) and that Boarelli should no longer be followed. . . . The majority judgment is that of McLachlin J. The essence of her reasoning is, in my view, to be found in this passage at p. 963-4:
The trend away from a moralistic view of tort suggests that the process of assessing damages should focus not on how the tortfeasor may be appropriately punished, but rather on what the injured person requires to restore him to his pre-accident state. To focus on the alleged "benefit" to the tortfeasor resulting from bringing collateral payments into account is to misconstrue the essential goal of the tort system. The law of tort is intended to restore the injured person to the position he enjoyed prior to the injury, rather than to punish the tortfeasor whose only wrong may have been a moment of inadvertence.
I conclude that the general principles underlying our system of tort law suggest that the damages awarded to the plaintiff should be confined to his or her actual loss, as closely as that can be calculated. The damages should be in an amount which will restore the plaintiff to his pre-accident position. Where pecuniary losses, such as loss of earnings, are at stake, the measure of damages is normally the plaintiff's actual financial loss. Unless the plaintiff can demonstrate such loss, he or she is not entitled to recover. This is because an essential element of tortious liability is lacking in the absence of loss. As Lord Diplock stated in Browning v. War Office, [1962] 3 All E.R. 1089, at pp. 1094-95: "A person who acts without reasonable care does no wrong in law; he commits no tort.
He only does wrong, he only commits a tort, if his lack of care causes damage to the plaintiff." McLachlin J., in her discussion of Boarelli at p. 969, referred to it as having "adopted a broad non-deductibility approach". In doing so, the court gave effect to the "moralistic view of tort" which focuses on punishment to the tortfeasor and on the supposed "benefit" to the tortfeasor which results from bringing collateral payments into account. That aspect was emphasised in Boarelli as in this passage at p. 8: ...I do not think that the Legislature intended them [welfare payments] to be for the benefit of the wrongdoer .... I therefore conclude that Boarelli was overruled in its entirety by Ratych v. Bloomer.
[140] In my opinion, authorities in the English Courts decided over the past several years have generally favoured the deductibility of social assistance payments from awards for loss of income: see Hodgson v. Trapp, [1989] 1 A.C. 807 and Lincoln v. Hayman, [1982] 2 All E.R. 819 (C.A.). As I interpret the reasoning in those cases, it was held that it would result in overcompensation of a plaintiff if the benefits received were not taken into account.
[141] It was not specifically necessary in the Ratych case for the majority to determine whether or not Boarelli should be overruled. However, I tend to agree with the view expressed by Esson J.A. in M.(M.) v. F.(R.), supra, that the reasoning in the majority judgment would appear to indicate such a result. I note this comment in the Reasons of the majority in Ratych, supra, at pp. 973-74:
[I]t may be that there is a valid distinction between cases where a person has prudently obtained and paid for personal insurance and cases where the benefits flow from the employer/employee relationship. The law has long recognized that in the first situation an exception should be made to the usual rule against double recovery. The existence of such an exception does not mean it should be extended to situations where personal prudence and deprivation are not demonstrated. In the latter case there is little to be weighed in the balance against the general policy of the law against double compensation. [Emphasis added.]
[142] There is no doubt that the private insurance exception, or an analogous exception such as was found to exist in the disability plans under consideration in Cunningham, supra, and related cases, are well-recognized exceptions to the rule against double recovery in tort cases. In these types of cases, the plaintiff has paid or given up something in order to receive the benefits. Neither can there be any doubt, however, that the basic rule is against double recovery and that the exceptions are truly exceptions.
[143] While social assistance benefits may be paid in this province to persons who are impoverished for a variety of reasons, it is clear from the legislative scheme that the payments are designed to provide income assistance. In the instant case, the plaintiff respondent required income assistance over many years because she had suffered psychological injury as a result of abuse and was rendered less capable of obtaining employment and earning income as a result. There is no question but that she received benefits as "income replacement." As I have noted, she claimed in this action that she was, because of the tort, less able to earn income by reasons of her injuries. She claimed for past and future loss of income. The trial judge made awards under those heads of damages.
[144] In my judgment, the social assistance payments the respondent received were a partial replacement of her income loss, or her capacity to earn income. These payments received by her do not fall within the insurance or pension exceptions. Nor in my view, do they have the character of charitable payments. This was not a situation similar to that in Redpath, supra, where a subscription was organized for the victims of a misfortune. Rather, it is a situation where payments were made to the respondent pursuant to a statutory income assistance scheme. I am in agreement with Mackenzie J.A. that these payments should not be categorized as within the charitable payments exception.
Therefore, in my judgment, the trial judge did not err in making the deduction she did from the past loss of income award. It follows that I would not accede to the respondent's argument that we ought to overrule M.(M.) v. F.(R.), referred to supra. In my view, that case was correctly decided.

treatments.proposition: The M.(M.) majority held retained social assistance deductible from past wage loss because Ratych had displaced Boarelli and welfare did not fit the charitable-gifts exception.
treatments.treatment: Prowse J.A. overruled M.(M.) on welfare deductibility because it assumed the payments duplicated the same loss and construed the charitable rationale too narrowly.

The final two cases to which I will refer are the decisions of this Court in M.(M.) and Jones v. Trudel. As earlier noted, Madam Justice Levine followed the M.(M.) decision in concluding that the social assistance benefits paid to M.B. should be deducted from the award for past loss of earning capacity.
[38] M.(M.) bore some similarities to this case in that it involved the assessment of damages in relation to the victim of sexual abuse perpetrated upon her by the son of her foster parents between 1969 and 1978. The action was brought by the plaintiff against both the son and the foster mother. The action against the son succeeded; the action against the foster mother was dismissed.
[39] The trial judge made no award for past wage loss on the basis that the social assistance benefits received by the plaintiff prior to trial were roughly equivalent to what she would have earned had the abuse not occurred and were deductible under that head of damage. The trial judge concluded that the reasoning in Boarelli on this point had been overruled by the majority decision in Ratych. On appeal, the plaintiff argued, amongst other things, that the trial judge erred in deducting social assistance benefits from the award for past wage loss on the basis that these benefits fell within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery.
[40] In this Court, Mr. Justice Esson, speaking for the majority, agreed with the trial judge that the reasoning upon which Boarelli was based with respect to the deductibility of welfare benefits had been overruled by the majority in Ratych. Mr. Justice Esson went on, however, to consider the question of whether these benefits were, nonetheless, non-deductible on the basis that they fell within the charitable gifts exception to double recovery. Esson J.A. quoted the passage from Madam Justice McLachlin's reasons in Cunningham which I have quoted at para. 26 above. In the result, he concluded that social assistance benefits did not fall within the rationale given by McLachlin J. for the charitable gifts exception. At para. 166 of M.(M.), Esson J.A. stated:
The importance of this passage [from Cunningham] is in explaining the rationale for exempting charitable gifts from the rule against double recovery. Primarily, it rests on the concern that "people" should not be discouraged from aiding those in misfortune. Secondarily, it reflects the reality that fixing the value of such assistance would be more trouble than it is worth. Neither of those considerations, in my view, can apply to welfare payments. I am, therefore, in agreement with the conclusion of the trial judge that such payments are not an exception to the general rule against allowing double recovery.
[41] In dissenting reasons, Mr. Justice Donald concluded that Boarelli had not been overruled by the majority in Ratych and that, in any event, social assistance benefits were sufficiently analogous to charitable gifts that they should be included in the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery.
[42] In his discussion of the Boarelli decision, Mr. Justice Donald noted that, in England, the question of the deductibility of social assistance benefits, which had been left open by Lord Reid in Parry v. Cleaver, had been answered in favour of deductibility in the later decision of the English Court of Appeal in Lincoln v. Hayman. (It does not appear that Hodgson v. Trapp was drawn to the attention of the Court.)
[43] Mr. Justice Donald did not find the Lincoln decision (discussed above at para. 31 above) persuasive. He noted that Lincoln did not consider cases involving intentional torts, such as sexual assault, where it could not be assumed that there would be an institutional insurer to spread the loss. Further, he noted that there was no basis for finding that social assistance benefits were sufficiently generous in Canada that victims of torts would be likely to delay their trials so that they could benefit from double recovery in the event that these benefits were not deducted. (I agree with Mr.
Justice Donald that this seems highly improbable given the subsistence level at which many of those on social assistance exist.) Finally, he noted that the public response to double recovery might well be different in cases of sexual assault where the public would likely regard the offender as unfairly benefiting from the social safety net at the expense of the victim in the event the benefits were deductible.
[44] Mr. Justice Donald noted that Ratych and Cunningham dealt with wage benefits and that, although Madam Justice McLachlin in Ratych disapproved the broad-based deductibility approach taken by the court in Boarelli, she did not reject the analysis of the decision insofar as it dealt with the deductibility of welfare payments.
[45] Finally, Mr. Justice Donald examined the nature and scope of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 27, and drew the following conclusions from that legislation (at paras. 85 and 86):
Two points arise from a consideration of the nature and scope of the Act. The scheme is society's collective response to the needs of the poor, a task once undertaken by religious institutions but now thought to be more effectively discharged by a public agency with a stable funding base provided by all taxpayers. The scheme arises from the notion that we are our brothers' keepers and that we must show compassion for the poor. In that sense the scheme is undoubtedly charitable in nature and clearly falls within the recognized exception in Boarelli. The second point is that welfare takes myriad forms, all of which have a value and cost.
If direct payments are to be deducted, what about the other benefits that may be provided such as social services, housing, health care, day care and so on? Arguably, the full value of the package of benefits received by a tort claimant would have to be deducted, because in principle they replace what an income from employment would purchase. This would be highly problematic in assessing damages. In my view, it is inappropriate to deduct welfare benefits of any kind.
[46] In summary, Mr. Justice Donald found that social assistance benefits should be treated as falling under the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery.
[47] M.(M.) was considered by this Court in Jones v. Trudel. There, the plaintiff was injured in a motor vehicle accident and received over $32,000 in social assistance payments prior to trial. Counsel had agreed that these payments would be repaid to the Ministry of Human Resources. The trial judge, therefore, did not deduct the amount of the payments received from the award for past loss of income. Her order included a term that the amount of "$32,184.00 of the aforesaid award for past income loss be paid by the Defendant to the Plaintiff in trust for the Ministry of Human Resources, representing social assistance benefits received by the Plaintiff." This Court upheld the trial judge's decision. In so doing, Mr.
Justice Lambert, speaking for the majority, commented on the M.(M.) decision as follows (at para. 55):
The applicable principles are settled for this Court by our judgment in M.(M) v. F.(R.) (1997), 101 B.C.A.C. 97 (B.C.C.A.). The majority in that case decided that in order to prevent double recovery the amount of welfare payments received and retained should be deducted from the amount awarded for past wage loss in relation to the period when the welfare payments were being received. But it is important to understand that there is a principled reason for making that deduction. It is made in order to prevent what the majority considered to be improper double recovery. If there is to be no double recovery, the principle could not apply. Mr. Justice Esson, for himself and Mr. Justice Cumming, made that clear, at para. 166, where he said:
In many, perhaps, most, cases where plaintiffs have been in receipt of welfare payments prior to trial, no question of double recovery will arise because, as in Boarelli [supra], the plaintiff will have made an assignment to the government body. So it is not the receipt of welfare during the past wage loss period that brings into operation the principle of avoidance of double recovery. Rather, it is the retention of the welfare amount and the intention to continue to retain the welfare amount, notwithstanding an award for past wage loss, which brings the principle of avoidance of double recovery into operation.

Before addressing the question of whether receipt of social assistance benefits by M.B. falls within one of the exceptions to the rule against double recovery, I must first address the question of whether the receipt of such benefits would result in double recovery. Unless the social assistance benefits duplicate damages under a particular head of damage in the tort award, it cannot be said that retention of them would result in double recovery. Thus, in this case, unless the social assistance benefits are a form of wage or earnings replacement, then it cannot be said that M.B. has been overcompensated by being paid twice for the same loss.
It does not appear that this argument was made in either M.(M.) or Jones, which apparently proceeded on the assumption

I agree with Mr. Justice Donald in M.(M.) that the nature and purpose of social assistance benefits are fundamentally charitable in that they are designed to provide assistance to those in need, however that need arises. In the case of social assistance benefits, however, the source of benevolence is not individuals, but the state. The state, in turn, funds this benevolence through the tax-paying public.
[78] It is true that the provision of social assistance benefits to victims of torts differs from the provision of a basket of groceries by a neighbour, or from the provision of disaster relief funds, in that the victim has no legal entitlement to the groceries or to moneys from the fund, whereas the victim of a tort may be entitled to social assistance if the financial and other legislative criteria are met. (As Mackenzie J.A. observes in his reasons for judgment, the concept of entitlement is reinforced by reference to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, U.N. Doc. A/810 (1948) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights 1966, U.N. Doc.
A/6316, Articles 9 and 11.) I note, however, that the entitlement to social assistance benefits is founded primarily on poverty, or need, the same foundation as for other charitable gifts. In that regard, I would reiterate the following passage from the judgment of Mr. Justice Donald in M.(M.), in which he discusses the nature of the provision of social assistance benefits under the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act (at para. 85):
The [social assistance] scheme is society's collective response to the needs of the poor, a task once undertaken by religious institutions but now thought to be more effectively discharged by a public agency with a stable funding base provided by all taxpayers. The scheme arises from the notion that we are our brothers' keepers and that we must show compassion for the poor. In that sense the scheme is undoubtedly charitable in nature and clearly falls within the recognized exception in Boarelli.
[79] I recognize that the aspect of entitlement to these benefits distinguishes them from traditional concepts of charity to the extent that they cannot be said to fall directly within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. In my view, however, they are sufficiently analogous to charity in all other respects that they can be reasonably brought under the umbrella of this exception.
[80] In answer to the view of the majority in M.(M.) that, unlike valuing other charitable gifts, valuing social assistance benefits does not present a problem, I agree with Mr. Justice Donald that social assistance benefits are myriad in form and that, if the value of all benefits were to be taken into account and deducted from a tort award, the task would be daunting.
[81] In response to the suggestion that this problem could be met by deducting only the moneys actually paid, rather than the value of the services provided, I note that isolating the payments which were solely for the benefit of the victim of the tort could be time-consuming in all cases except those where the recipient had no dependants throughout the relevant period, such that it could be said that the benefits were provided for that person and that person alone. In this case, for example, M.B. was single for part of the payment period, had one child for part of the period, had two children for part of the period, and was living with another individual (also a social assistance recipient) for part of the period.
The only evidence before the Court of the amounts she received are total figures received during a particular period. They are not broken down according to her living arrangements at any point in time. In that respect, valuing these benefits may present even greater difficulties than valuing other charitable gifts.
[82] In summary, I do not agree with the majority in M.(M.) that social assistance benefits cannot be brought within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. The exception is expanded somewhat in so doing, but in my view, the principles underlying the exception justify this expansion.
[83] In coming to this conclusion, I concur with Lord Bridge in Hodgson that public policy weighs heavily in the determination of whether benefits, such as the social assistance benefits provided in this case, should be deducted from tort awards in order to avoid double recovery. In that regard, the Legislature has far more resources available to it to gather in and weigh the information necessary to make such decisions than does the judiciary. Even with the resources available to it, the Ontario Law Reform Commission did not feel it had the empirical evidence necessary to make a recommendation with respect to this issue.
[84] Similarly, in its wide-ranging report on the deductibility of collateral benefits in England (excepting social assistance benefits which had already been dealt with by legislation) the English Law Reform Commission found that there was not sufficient consensus amongst the many groups consulted with respect to any of its proposed options for reform to justify recommendations for further legislative changes. (See Law Commission, Damages for Personal Injury: Medical, Nursing and Other Expenses; Collateral Benefits, Report No. 262 (November 1999).)
[85] The only community which seems relatively united in its position with respect to the deductibility of collateral benefits, including social assistance benefits, is the academic community. It favours deductibility of all collateral benefits on the basis that any form of overcompensation or double recovery cannot be justified in relation to the fundamental goal of damages which is to provide the victim with full compensation, but no more.
[86] I would add, however, that there are many who believe that full compensation for damages suffered by victims of torts has been, and continues to be, unattainable under our present system. This view was voiced by Peter Andrews, Q.C. in his submission to the English Law Commission that all collateral benefits should be ignored in the assessment of damages for tort. He expressed his views as follows (at p. 133, Law Com. Report):
. . . in many cases of serious personal injury, the plaintiff does not receive truly compensatory damages. He is not placed in the same position as if uninjured. It then follows that there should be no general principle debarring him from retaining "accident" moneys whatever the source. There will be no double recovery because tort damages are only one of the layers of protection which society should provide to those who are disabled.
Different members of society will accumulate different levels of recompense for similar injuries depending on a variety of factors, including but not limited to charity donations, personal insurance, the quality of the employment contract, the competence of the instructed lawyers, the idiosyncrasies of the determining judge, and the chance of whether the accident is susceptible to tortious recovery.
Although this point of view was regarded by the Law Commissioners as somewhat of "a counsel of despair", it was recognized as raising a valid concern about whether full compensation for the victims of tort is ever achieved in practice.
[87] In the United States for many years, the general rule was that there should be no deduction for collateral benefits, no matter what the source. This position was influenced, in large part, by the fact that it was well known that lawyers' fees were payable from damage awards, with the result that the amount received by the victim of a tort would never be fully compensatory. (I have little doubt that the same pertains in Canada.) The movement away from non-deductibility in some states in later years has stemmed largely from the astronomical size of jury damage awards, a problem which has not reached a similar magnitude in Canada to date.
[88] In British Columbia, based on the legislation pursuant to which these benefits were paid, I am satisfied that social assistance benefits, while differing in some respects from traditional examples of charitable gifts, are sufficiently analogous to be brought within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. I would, therefore, overrule the prior decisions of this Court in M.(M.) and Jones

treatments.treatment: Prowse J.A. adopted the dissent's account of the benefits' charitable purpose and extended the charitable-gifts exception to them.

treatments.proposition: M.(M.) treated welfare and an earnings-loss award as double compensation under Ratych.
treatments.treatment: Mackenzie J.A. held that M.(M.) misconceived the threshold inquiry because assistance responds to need across different periods while tort damages compensate earning-capacity loss attributable to particular torts.

supporting_passages.text: I agree with her conclusion that the social insurance benefits received by the plaintiff should not be deducted from the award of damages for loss of earning capacity. In my respectful view, the majority judgment of this court in M.(M.) v. F.(R.) (1997), 52 B.C.L.R.(3d) 127 (C.A.), was based on a misconception of the application of Ratych v. Bloomer, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 940, and should not be followed.

Ratych rejected the broad Boarelli principle of non-deductibility, but the deduction of social welfare benefits was not addressed. The case involved a claim for loss of earnings due to injury sustained in a motor vehicle accident where the plaintiff, a police officer, had been paid his full salary throughout from sick leave benefits to which he was entitled under the terms of his employment. McLachlin J. (now C.J.C.) for the majority framed the essential question as;
"how far is it right that a person should be compensated for the same loss from more than one source? (My emphasis.)
[104] Social welfare benefits are "income assistance" under the Act. Income assistance is defined as "a support and shelter allowance". Support and shelter connote need. They are independent of any loss. The trial judge assessed the loss of earning capacity caused by the assaults of the foster father and the biological father together at $10,000, after deducting income assistance of $122,320.96. This Court substituted $50,000 before income assistance reflecting a division between the separate torts of the foster father and the biological father. That loss is spread over the period of 20 years from 1979 when the plaintiff reached age 18 to the trial date in 1999. The income assistance of $122,320.96 was all received between September 1991 and November 1998.
The result of the trial judge's approach is that income assistance received in the 1991 to 1998 period is deducted, in part, from compensation for loss of earning capacity in the 1979 to 1990 period.
[105] I do not think that there is any authority for the proposition that social assistance benefits received in one period can be deducted from damages for loss of earnings suffered in a different period. Clearly it cannot be said to be compensation for the same loss. Factually, this case illustrates the issues of allocation that will arise from deductibility. Apart from the timing difficulties, there is the further problem noted by Prowse J.A. of dividing the benefits between the damages for the tort of the biological father, a claim that has been settled, and the tort of the foster father at issue here. I do not think there is any difference in principle between tortfeasors in terms of deductibility when each tort has contributed to the earnings loss.
[106] While these complications are specific to the present case, they illustrate the difficulties facing deductibility of social assistance benefits more generally. They underline the general proposition that damages and social assistance reflect different compensation objectives and there is no direct connection between them. In my opinion, they are not compensation for the same loss as the issue was framed in Ratych and consequently they do not pass the threshold requirement of double compensation. In my respectful view, the majority opinion in M.(M.) assumed double compensation and in that respect misapplied Ratych.

the threshold test, affirmed in Ratych, is that a deductible benefit must be paid for the same loss. Social assistance benefits are identified with need: they are not an indemnity for the loss claimed in the action. In my view, the threshold test has not been met and the benefits paid to the plaintiff are not deductible.

treatments.proposition: The M.(M.) majority treated social assistance as double recovery rather than as wage replacement serving a different objective.
treatments.treatment: Finch C.J.B.C. expressly rejected the majority view because social assistance and tort damages serve different compensatory purposes.

supporting_passages.text: I expressly agree with Madam Justice Prowse and Mr. Justice Mackenzie that the social security benefits paid to the plaintiff in this case do not give rise to double recovery for loss of income, because those benefits are not in the nature of wage or income replacement. As Mr. Justice Mackenzie says, the two sources of payment reflect different compensation objectives. I respectfully disagree with the majority view in M.(M.) v. F.(R.) (1997), 52 B.C.L.R. (3d) 127.

treatments.proposition: Donald J.A.'s M.(M.) dissent treated social assistance as falling within the charitable-gifts exception.
treatments.treatment: Finch C.J.B.C. adopted that dissent as an alternative ground for non-deductibility.

supporting_passages.text: I also agree with Madam Justice Prowse that social security benefits would come within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery, for the dissenting reasons expressed by Mr. Justice Donald in M.(M.).

treatments.proposition: M.(M.) read Ratych's actual-loss rule as requiring welfare payments that replace income to be deducted.
treatments.treatment: Hall J.A. agreed with M.(M.) and applied Ratych's actual-loss reasoning because the assistance replaced income and fit no exception.

supporting_passages.text:
the respondent argues that we should overrule the following conclusions expressed by Esson J.A., speaking for the majority, in the case of M.(M.) v. F.(R.) (1999), 52 B.C.L.R. (3d) 127 (C.A.) at pp. 181-82:
The final question is that as to the deductibility of welfare benefits. The Ontario Court of Appeal, in Boarelli v. Flannigan (1973), 36 D.L.R. (3d) 4 (Ont. C.A.) held that such benefits are not to be deducted. I agree with the learned trial judge that the reasoning upon which that decision was based was overruled by the Supreme Court of Canada in Ratych v. Bloomer, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 940 (S.C.C.) and that Boarelli should no longer be followed. . . . The majority judgment is that of McLachlin J. The essence of her reasoning is, in my view, to be found in this passage at p. 963-4:
The trend away from a moralistic view of tort suggests that the process of assessing damages should focus not on how the tortfeasor may be appropriately punished, but rather on what the injured person requires to restore him to his pre-accident state. To focus on the alleged "benefit" to the tortfeasor resulting from bringing collateral payments into account is to misconstrue the essential goal of the tort system. The law of tort is intended to restore the injured person to the position he enjoyed prior to the injury, rather than to punish the tortfeasor whose only wrong may have been a moment of inadvertence.
I conclude that the general principles underlying our system of tort law suggest that the damages awarded to the plaintiff should be confined to his or her actual loss, as closely as that can be calculated. The damages should be in an amount which will restore the plaintiff to his pre-accident position. Where pecuniary losses, such as loss of earnings, are at stake, the measure of damages is normally the plaintiff's actual financial loss. Unless the plaintiff can demonstrate such loss, he or she is not entitled to recover. This is because an essential element of tortious liability is lacking in the absence of loss. As Lord Diplock stated in Browning v. War Office, [1962] 3 All E.R. 1089, at pp. 1094-95: "A person who acts without reasonable care does no wrong in law; he commits no tort.
He only does wrong, he only commits a tort, if his lack of care causes damage to the plaintiff." McLachlin J., in her discussion of Boarelli at p. 969, referred to it as having "adopted a broad non-deductibility approach". In doing so, the court gave effect to the "moralistic view of tort" which focuses on punishment to the tortfeasor and on the supposed "benefit" to the tortfeasor which results from bringing collateral payments into account. That aspect was emphasised in Boarelli as in this passage at p. 8: ...I do not think that the Legislature intended them [welfare payments] to be for the benefit of the wrongdoer .... I therefore conclude that Boarelli was overruled in its entirety by Ratych v. Bloomer.

I tend to agree with the view expressed by Esson J.A. in M.(M.) v. F.(R.), supra, that the reasoning in the majority judgment would appear to indicate such a result. I note this comment in the Reasons of the majority in Ratych, supra, at pp. 973-74:
[I]t may be that there is a valid distinction between cases where a person has prudently obtained and paid for personal insurance and cases where the benefits flow from the employer/employee relationship. The law has long recognized that in the first situation an exception should be made to the usual rule against double recovery. The existence of such an exception does not mean it should be extended to situations where personal prudence and deprivation are not demonstrated. In the latter case there is little to be weighed in the balance against the general policy of the law against double compensation. [Emphasis added.]
[142] There is no doubt that the private insurance exception, or an analogous exception such as was found to exist in the disability plans under consideration in Cunningham, supra, and related cases, are well-recognized exceptions to the rule against double recovery in tort cases. In these types of cases, the plaintiff has paid or given up something in order to receive the benefits. Neither can there be any doubt, however, that the basic rule is against double recovery and that the exceptions are truly exceptions.
[143] While social assistance benefits may be paid in this province to persons who are impoverished for a variety of reasons, it is clear from the legislative scheme that the payments are designed to provide income assistance. In the instant case, the plaintiff respondent required income assistance over many years because she had suffered psychological injury as a result of abuse and was rendered less capable of obtaining employment and earning income as a result. There is no question but that she received benefits as "income replacement." As I have noted, she claimed in this action that she was, because of the tort, less able to earn income by reasons of her injuries. She claimed for past and future loss of income. The trial judge made awards under those heads of damages.
[144] In my judgment, the social assistance payments the respondent received were a partial replacement of her income loss, or her capacity to earn income. These payments received by her do not fall within the insurance or pension exceptions. Nor in my view, do they have the character of charitable payments. This was not a situation similar to that in Redpath, supra, where a subscription was organized for the victims of a misfortune. Rather, it is a situation where payments were made to the respondent pursuant to a statutory income assistance scheme. I am in agreement with Mackenzie J.A. that these payments should not be categorized as within the charitable payments exception.
Therefore, in my judgment, the trial judge did not err in making the deduction she did from the past loss of income award. It follows that I would not accede to the respondent's argument that we ought to overrule M.(M.) v. F.(R.), referred to supra. In my view, that case was correctly decided.

C.A.) held that such benefits are not to be deducted. I agree with the learned trial judge that the reasoning upon which that decision was based was overruled by the Supreme Court of Canada in Ratych v. Bloomer, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 940 (S.C.C.) and that Boarelli should no longer be followed. . . . The majority judgment is that of McLachlin J. The essence of her reasoning is, in my view, to be found in this passage at p. 963-4:
The trend away from a moralistic view of tort suggests that the process of assessing damages should focus not on how the tortfeasor may be appropriately punished, but rather on what the injured person requires to restore him to his pre-accident state. To focus on the alleged "benefit" to the tortfeasor resulting from bringing collateral payments into account is to misconstrue the essential goal of the tort system. The law of tort is intended to restore the injured person to the position he enjoyed prior to the injury, rather than to punish the tortfeasor whose only wrong may have been a moment of inadvertence.
I conclude that the general principles underlying our system of tort law suggest that the damages awarded to the plaintiff should be confined to his or her actual loss, as closely as that can be calculated. The damages should be in an amount which will restore the plaintiff to his pre-accident position. Where pecuniary losses, such as loss of earnings, are at stake, the measure of damages is normally the plaintiff's actual financial loss. Unless the plaintiff can demonstrate such loss, he or she is not entitled to recover. This is because an essential element of tortious liability is lacking in the absence of loss.
