I think the exemption for the private policy of insurance should be maintained. It has a long history. It is understood and accepted. There has never been any confusion as to when it should be applied. More importantly it is based on fairness. All who insure themselves for disability benefits are displaying wisdom and forethought in making provision for the continuation of some income in case of disabling injury or illness. The acquisition of the policy has social benefits for those insured, their dependants and indeed their community. It represents forbearance and self-denial on the part of the purchaser of the policy to provide for contingencies. They involve no element of individual forbearance, self-denial, or forethought by recipients - they are funded by the taxpayers generally and anyone who satisfies the qualifying criteria is entitled to receive them.

Bloomer, supra, and of Cunningham v. Wheeler, supra, is that all collateral payments in the nature of income that have been received by a plaintiff must be taken into account in an award of damages for past loss of income unless they fall within the private insurance or charitable exceptions.

I conclude that the general principles underlying our system of tort law suggest that the damages awarded to the plaintiff should be confined to his or her actual loss, as closely as that can be calculated. The damages should be in an amount which will restore the plaintiff to his pre-accident position. Where pecuniary losses, such as loss of earnings, are at stake, the measure of damages is normally the plaintiff's actual financial loss. Unless the plaintiff can demonstrate such loss, he or she is not entitled to recover. As Lord Diplock stated in Browning v. War Office, [1962] 3 All E.R. 1089, at pp. 1094-95: "A person who acts without reasonable care does no wrong in law; he commits no tort. He only does wrong, he only commits a tort, if his lack of care causes damage to the plaintiff."
[152] Of course, if the collateral payer is entitled to be subrogated to the plaintiff's claim, the collateral payments cannot offset the plaintiff's loss. The right to subrogation is normally created by contract, as in the case of private insurance, or by statute, as in the case of some statutory benefits. Subrogation may also be achieved by the courts through the imposition of a trust upon an award or by a direction to pay in favour of persons in close relationship to the plaintiff who have gratuitously provided necessary services, such as nursing care: see Ratych v. Bloomer, supra, at 978-79. As McLachlin J. said at 979, the justification for such court-imposed subrogation:
... may be seen as a moral obligation on the part of the injured plaintiff to repay those who rendered services to him gratuitously, coupled with the desirability of avoiding the injustice which would result from the inability to otherwise compensate the persons who rendered services, given that they had no independent cause of action.
[153] In such cases, the loss caused by the tort has been conditionally absorbed by the collateral payer and restitution of the payer's loss is accomplished derivatively through the plaintiff's claim against the tortfeasor. Thus, it is not the plaintiff's loss at all. If the plaintiff does not recover from the tortfeasor, the collateral payer suffers the loss. If the plaintiff does recover, the payer's loss is recompensed by the tortfeasor.
[154] When subrogation is not a relevant consideration, it must be determined whether the collateral payments were received on account of the plaintiff's loss. To the extent that they were so received, the plaintiff's loss has been recompensed and the tortfeasor cannot be called upon to pay.
[155] The relevant pre-trial damage alleged by the plaintiff in her statement of claim in this case was "a loss of income." Although, the trial judge characterized the claim as one for "loss of earning capacity", it is my view that the effect of her award was to replace a lost income stream. The trial judge implicitly recognized this as the essence of the award when she based it upon statistical evidence of average employment earnings of females resident in British Columbia (see her reasons at [2000] B.C.J. No. 909 (Q.L.), para. 310). Moreover, this view is consistent with fundamental principle. The measure of damages is the plaintiff's actual financial loss, not the theoretical value of an untapped abstract capacity to earn.
In my view, the difference in phraseology in respect of pre-trial loss between "loss of income" and "loss of earning capacity" is terminological, not substantive.
[156] Consequently, the award of damages for pre-trial loss of income in this case has converted a past uncertainty into a certainty - but for her tortiously-caused injuries, the plaintiff would have been employed during the pre-trial period and would have earned income from her employment.
[157] The corollary of this conclusion is that the plaintiff would not have received income assistance benefits while she was working. It is implicit in the deduction of the income assistance payments by the trial judge that, as a matter of fact, the plaintiff would not have been eligible to receive them while she was gainfully employed. It follows that the income assistance payments that the plaintiff received had the effect of partially replacing her lost employment income.

The final two cases to which I will refer are the decisions of this Court in M.(M.) and Jones v. Trudel. As earlier noted, Madam Justice Levine followed the M.(M.) decision in concluding that the social assistance benefits paid to M.B. should be deducted from the award for past loss of earning capacity.
[38] M.(M.) bore some similarities to this case in that it involved the assessment of damages in relation to the victim of sexual abuse perpetrated upon her by the son of her foster parents between 1969 and 1978. The action was brought by the plaintiff against both the son and the foster mother. The action against the son succeeded; the action against the foster mother was dismissed.
[39] The trial judge made no award for past wage loss on the basis that the social assistance benefits received by the plaintiff prior to trial were roughly equivalent to what she would have earned had the abuse not occurred and were deductible under that head of damage. The trial judge concluded that the reasoning in Boarelli on this point had been overruled by the majority decision in Ratych. On appeal, the plaintiff argued, amongst other things, that the trial judge erred in deducting social assistance benefits from the award for past wage loss on the basis that these benefits fell within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery.
[40] In this Court, Mr. Justice Esson, speaking for the majority, agreed with the trial judge that the reasoning upon which Boarelli was based with respect to the deductibility of welfare benefits had been overruled by the majority in Ratych. Mr. Justice Esson went on, however, to consider the question of whether these benefits were, nonetheless, non-deductible on the basis that they fell within the charitable gifts exception to double recovery. Esson J.A. quoted the passage from Madam Justice McLachlin's reasons in Cunningham which I have quoted at para. 26 above. In the result, he concluded that social assistance benefits did not fall within the rationale given by McLachlin J. for the charitable gifts exception. At para. 166 of M.(M.), Esson J.A. stated:
The importance of this passage [from Cunningham] is in explaining the rationale for exempting charitable gifts from the rule against double recovery. Primarily, it rests on the concern that "people" should not be discouraged from aiding those in misfortune. Secondarily, it reflects the reality that fixing the value of such assistance would be more trouble than it is worth. Neither of those considerations, in my view, can apply to welfare payments. I am, therefore, in agreement with the conclusion of the trial judge that such payments are not an exception to the general rule against allowing double recovery.
[41] In dissenting reasons, Mr. Justice Donald concluded that Boarelli had not been overruled by the majority in Ratych and that, in any event, social assistance benefits were sufficiently analogous to charitable gifts that they should be included in the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery.
[42] In his discussion of the Boarelli decision, Mr. Justice Donald noted that, in England, the question of the deductibility of social assistance benefits, which had been left open by Lord Reid in Parry v. Cleaver, had been answered in favour of deductibility in the later decision of the English Court of Appeal in Lincoln v. Hayman. (It does not appear that Hodgson v. Trapp was drawn to the attention of the Court.)
[43] Mr. Justice Donald did not find the Lincoln decision (discussed above at para. 31 above) persuasive. He noted that Lincoln did not consider cases involving intentional torts, such as sexual assault, where it could not be assumed that there would be an institutional insurer to spread the loss. Further, he noted that there was no basis for finding that social assistance benefits were sufficiently generous in Canada that victims of torts would be likely to delay their trials so that they could benefit from double recovery in the event that these benefits were not deducted. (I agree with Mr.
Justice Donald that this seems highly improbable given the subsistence level at which many of those on social assistance exist.) Finally, he noted that the public response to double recovery might well be different in cases of sexual assault where the public would likely regard the offender as unfairly benefiting from the social safety net at the expense of the victim in the event the benefits were deductible.
[44] Mr. Justice Donald noted that Ratych and Cunningham dealt with wage benefits and that, although Madam Justice McLachlin in Ratych disapproved the broad-based deductibility approach taken by the court in Boarelli, she did not reject the analysis of the decision insofar as it dealt with the deductibility of welfare payments.
[45] Finally, Mr. Justice Donald examined the nature and scope of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 27, and drew the following conclusions from that legislation (at paras. 85 and 86):
Two points arise from a consideration of the nature and scope of the Act. The scheme is society's collective response to the needs of the poor, a task once undertaken by religious institutions but now thought to be more effectively discharged by a public agency with a stable funding base provided by all taxpayers. The scheme arises from the notion that we are our brothers' keepers and that we must show compassion for the poor. In that sense the scheme is undoubtedly charitable in nature and clearly falls within the recognized exception in Boarelli. The second point is that welfare takes myriad forms, all of which have a value and cost.
If direct payments are to be deducted, what about the other benefits that may be provided such as social services, housing, health care, day care and so on? Arguably, the full value of the package of benefits received by a tort claimant would have to be deducted, because in principle they replace what an income from employment would purchase. This would be highly problematic in assessing damages. In my view, it is inappropriate to deduct welfare benefits of any kind.
[46] In summary, Mr. Justice Donald found that social assistance benefits should be treated as falling under the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery.
[47] M.(M.) was considered by this Court in Jones v. Trudel. There, the plaintiff was injured in a motor vehicle accident and received over $32,000 in social assistance payments prior to trial. Counsel had agreed that these payments would be repaid to the Ministry of Human Resources. The trial judge, therefore, did not deduct the amount of the payments received from the award for past loss of income. Her order included a term that the amount of "$32,184.00 of the aforesaid award for past income loss be paid by the Defendant to the Plaintiff in trust for the Ministry of Human Resources, representing social assistance benefits received by the Plaintiff." This Court upheld the trial judge's decision. In so doing, Mr.
Justice Lambert, speaking for the majority, commented on the M.(M.) decision as follows (at para. 55):
The applicable principles are settled for this Court by our judgment in M.(M) v. F.(R.) (1997), 101 B.C.A.C. 97 (B.C.C.A.). The majority in that case decided that in order to prevent double recovery the amount of welfare payments received and retained should be deducted from the amount awarded for past wage loss in relation to the period when the welfare payments were being received. But it is important to understand that there is a principled reason for making that deduction. It is made in order to prevent what the majority considered to be improper double recovery. If there is to be no double recovery, the principle could not apply. Mr. Justice Esson, for himself and Mr. Justice Cumming, made that clear, at para. 166, where he said:
In many, perhaps, most, cases where plaintiffs have been in receipt of welfare payments prior to trial, no question of double recovery will arise because, as in Boarelli [supra], the plaintiff will have made an assignment to the government body. So it is not the receipt of welfare during the past wage loss period that brings into operation the principle of avoidance of double recovery. Rather, it is the retention of the welfare amount and the intention to continue to retain the welfare amount, notwithstanding an award for past wage loss, which brings the principle of avoidance of double recovery into operation.
[48] According to both M.(M.) and Jones v. Trudel, therefore, Madam Justice Levine's decision to deduct

Before addressing the question of whether receipt of social assistance benefits by M.B. falls within one of the exceptions to the rule against double recovery, I must first address the question of whether the receipt of such benefits would result in double recovery. Unless the social assistance benefits duplicate damages under a particular head of damage in the tort award, it cannot be said that retention of them would result in double recovery. Thus, in this case, unless the social assistance benefits are a form of wage or earnings replacement, then it cannot be said that M.B. has been overcompensated by being paid twice for the same loss.
It does not appear that this argument was made in either M.(M.) or Jones, which apparently proceeded on the assumption

I agree with Mr. Justice Donald in M.(M.) that the nature and purpose of social assistance benefits are fundamentally charitable in that they are designed to provide assistance to those in need, however that need arises. In the case of social assistance benefits, however, the source of benevolence is not individuals, but the state. The state, in turn, funds this benevolence through the tax-paying public.
[78] It is true that the provision of social assistance benefits to victims of torts differs from the provision of a basket of groceries by a neighbour, or from the provision of disaster relief funds, in that the victim has no legal entitlement to the groceries or to moneys from the fund, whereas the victim of a tort may be entitled to social assistance if the financial and other legislative criteria are met. (As Mackenzie J.A. observes in his reasons for judgment, the concept of entitlement is reinforced by reference to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, U.N. Doc. A/810 (1948) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights 1966, U.N. Doc.
A/6316, Articles 9 and 11.) I note, however, that the entitlement to social assistance benefits is founded primarily on poverty, or need, the same foundation as for other charitable gifts. In that regard, I would reiterate the following passage from the judgment of Mr. Justice Donald in M.(M.), in which he discusses the nature of the provision of social assistance benefits under the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act (at para. 85):
The [social assistance] scheme is society's collective response to the needs of the poor, a task once undertaken by religious institutions but now thought to be more effectively discharged by a public agency with a stable funding base provided by all taxpayers. The scheme arises from the notion that we are our brothers' keepers and that we must show compassion for the poor. In that sense the scheme is undoubtedly charitable in nature and clearly falls within the recognized exception in Boarelli.
[79] I recognize that the aspect of entitlement to these benefits distinguishes them from traditional concepts of charity to the extent that they cannot be said to fall directly within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. In my view, however, they are sufficiently analogous to charity in all other respects that they can be reasonably brought under the umbrella of this exception.
[80] In answer to the view of the majority in M.(M.) that, unlike valuing other charitable gifts, valuing social assistance benefits does not present a problem, I agree with Mr. Justice Donald that social assistance benefits are myriad in form and that, if the value of all benefits were to be taken into account and deducted from a tort award, the task would be daunting.
[81] In response to the suggestion that this problem could be met by deducting only the moneys actually paid, rather than the value of the services provided, I note that isolating the payments which were solely for the benefit of the victim of the tort could be time-consuming in all cases except those where the recipient had no dependants throughout the relevant period, such that it could be said that the benefits were provided for that person and that person alone. In this case, for example, M.B. was single for part of the payment period, had one child for part of the period, had two children for part of the period, and was living with another individual (also a social assistance recipient) for part of the period.
The only evidence before the Court of the amounts she received are total figures received during a particular period. They are not broken down according to her living arrangements at any point in time. In that respect, valuing these benefits may present even greater difficulties than valuing other charitable gifts.
[82] In summary, I do not agree with the majority in M.(M.) that social assistance benefits cannot be brought within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. The exception is expanded somewhat in so doing, but in my view, the principles underlying the exception justify this expansion.
[83] In coming to this conclusion, I concur with Lord Bridge in Hodgson that public policy weighs heavily in the determination of whether benefits, such as the social assistance benefits provided in this case, should be deducted from tort awards in order to avoid double recovery. In that regard, the Legislature has far more resources available to it to gather in and weigh the information necessary to make such decisions than does the judiciary. Even with the resources available to it, the Ontario Law Reform Commission did not feel it had the empirical evidence necessary to make a recommendation with respect to this issue.
[84] Similarly, in its wide-ranging report on the deductibility of collateral benefits in England (excepting social assistance benefits which had already been dealt with by legislation) the English Law Reform Commission found that there was not sufficient consensus amongst the many groups consulted with respect to any of its proposed options for reform to justify recommendations for further legislative changes. (See Law Commission, Damages for Personal Injury: Medical, Nursing and Other Expenses; Collateral Benefits, Report No. 262 (November 1999).)
[85] The only community which seems relatively united in its position with respect to the deductibility of collateral benefits, including social assistance benefits, is the academic community. It favours deductibility of all collateral benefits on the basis that any form of overcompensation or double recovery cannot be justified in relation to the fundamental goal of damages which is to provide the victim with full compensation, but no more.
[86] I would add, however, that there are many who believe that full compensation for damages suffered by victims of torts has been, and continues to be, unattainable under our present system. This view was voiced by Peter Andrews, Q.C. in his submission to the English Law Commission that all collateral benefits should be ignored in the assessment of damages for tort. He expressed his views as follows (at p. 133, Law Com. Report):
. . . in many cases of serious personal injury, the plaintiff does not receive truly compensatory damages. He is not placed in the same position as if uninjured. It then follows that there should be no general principle debarring him from retaining "accident" moneys whatever the source. There will be no double recovery because tort damages are only one of the layers of protection which society should provide to those who are disabled.
Different members of society will accumulate different levels of recompense for similar injuries depending on a variety of factors, including but not limited to charity donations, personal insurance, the quality of the employment contract, the competence of the instructed lawyers, the idiosyncrasies of the determining judge, and the chance of whether the accident is susceptible to tortious recovery.
Although this point of view was regarded by the Law Commissioners as somewhat of "a counsel of despair", it was recognized as raising a valid concern about whether full compensation for the victims of tort is ever achieved in practice.
[87] In the United States for many years, the general rule was that there should be no deduction for collateral benefits, no matter what the source. This position was influenced, in large part, by the fact that it was well known that lawyers' fees were payable from damage awards, with the result that the amount received by the victim of a tort would never be fully compensatory. (I have little doubt that the same pertains in Canada.) The movement away from non-deductibility in some states in later years has stemmed largely from the astronomical size of jury damage awards, a problem which has not reached a similar magnitude in Canada to date.
[88] In British Columbia, based on the legislation pursuant to which these benefits were paid, I am satisfied that social assistance benefits, while differing in some respects from traditional examples of charitable gifts, are sufficiently analogous to be brought within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. I would, therefore, overrule the prior decisions of this Court in M.(M.) and Jones

treatments.treatment: Mackenzie J.A. accepted Jones's repayment rule but distinguished it because the Province had not pursued a repayment agreement with M.B.

supporting_passages.text:
There is one proposition that is uncontested in this otherwise controversial area of the law, namely that there is no deductibility if there is a right of subrogation. A benefit paid to a plaintiff is not deductible where the plaintiff is under an obligation to repay the benefit out of the tort award. This proposition is the narrow ratio of Boarelli v. Flannigan (1973), 36 D.L.R. (3d) 4, at 6 (Ont. C.A.) and it was treated as axiomatic in Ratych v. Bloomer and Cunningham v. Wheeler, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 359. It was also the ratio of the majority judgment in Jones v. Trudel (2000), 74 B.C.L.R.(3d) 263 (C.A.).
[102] No right of subrogation is claimed in this case. Section 12 of the BC Benefits (Income Assistance) Act, R.S.B.C. c. 27, authorizes the government to make subrogation agreements with social welfare recipients but these discretionary provisions have not been pursued.

Ratych rejected the broad Boarelli principle of non-deductibility, but the deduction of social welfare benefits was not addressed. The case involved a claim for loss of earnings due to injury sustained in a motor vehicle accident where the plaintiff, a police officer, had been paid his full salary throughout from sick leave benefits to which he was entitled under the terms of his employment. McLachlin J. (now C.J.C.) for the majority framed the essential question as;
"how far is it right that a person should be compensated for the same loss from more than one source? (My emphasis.)

the threshold test, affirmed in Ratych, is that a deductible benefit must be paid for the same loss. Social assistance benefits are identified with need: they are not an indemnity for the loss claimed in the action. In my view, the threshold test has not been met and the benefits paid to the plaintiff are not deductible.

the respondent argues that we should overrule the following conclusions expressed by Esson J.A., speaking for the majority, in the case of M.(M.) v. F.(R.) (1999), 52 B.C.L.R. (3d) 127 (C.A.) at pp. 181-82:
The final question is that as to the deductibility of welfare benefits. The Ontario Court of Appeal, in Boarelli v. Flannigan (1973), 36 D.L.R. (3d) 4 (Ont. C.A.) held that such benefits are not to be deducted. I agree with the learned trial judge that the reasoning upon which that decision was based was overruled by the Supreme Court of Canada in Ratych v. Bloomer, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 940 (S.C.C.) and that Boarelli should no longer be followed. . . . The majority judgment is that of McLachlin J. The essence of her reasoning is, in my view, to be found in this passage at p. 963-4:
The trend away from a moralistic view of tort suggests that the process of assessing damages should focus not on how the tortfeasor may be appropriately punished, but rather on what the injured person requires to restore him to his pre-accident state. To focus on the alleged "benefit" to the tortfeasor resulting from bringing collateral payments into account is to misconstrue the essential goal of the tort system. The law of tort is intended to restore the injured person to the position he enjoyed prior to the injury, rather than to punish the tortfeasor whose only wrong may have been a moment of inadvertence.
I conclude that the general principles underlying our system of tort law suggest that the damages awarded to the plaintiff should be confined to his or her actual loss, as closely as that can be calculated. The damages should be in an amount which will restore the plaintiff to his pre-accident position. Where pecuniary losses, such as loss of earnings, are at stake, the measure of damages is normally the plaintiff's actual financial loss. Unless the plaintiff can demonstrate such loss, he or she is not entitled to recover. This is because an essential element of tortious liability is lacking in the absence of loss. As Lord Diplock stated in Browning v. War Office, [1962] 3 All E.R. 1089, at pp. 1094-95: "A person who acts without reasonable care does no wrong in law; he commits no tort.
He only does wrong, he only commits a tort, if his lack of care causes damage to the plaintiff." McLachlin J., in her discussion of Boarelli at p. 969, referred to it as having "adopted a broad non-deductibility approach". In doing so, the court gave effect to the "moralistic view of tort" which focuses on punishment to the tortfeasor and on the supposed "benefit" to the tortfeasor which results from bringing collateral payments into account. That aspect was emphasised in Boarelli as in this passage at p. 8: ...I do not think that the Legislature intended them [welfare payments] to be for the benefit of the wrongdoer .... I therefore conclude that Boarelli was overruled in its entirety by Ratych v. Bloomer.

I tend to agree with the view expressed by Esson J.A. in M.(M.) v. F.(R.), supra, that the reasoning in the majority judgment would appear to indicate such a result. I note this comment in the Reasons of the majority in Ratych, supra, at pp. 973-74:
[I]t may be that there is a valid distinction between cases where a person has prudently obtained and paid for personal insurance and cases where the benefits flow from the employer/employee relationship. The law has long recognized that in the first situation an exception should be made to the usual rule against double recovery. The existence of such an exception does not mean it should be extended to situations where personal prudence and deprivation are not demonstrated. In the latter case there is little to be weighed in the balance against the general policy of the law against double compensation. [Emphasis added.]
[142] There is no doubt that the private insurance exception, or an analogous exception such as was found to exist in the disability plans under consideration in Cunningham, supra, and related cases, are well-recognized exceptions to the rule against double recovery in tort cases. In these types of cases, the plaintiff has paid or given up something in order to receive the benefits. Neither can there be any doubt, however, that the basic rule is against double recovery and that the exceptions are truly exceptions.
[143] While social assistance benefits may be paid in this province to persons who are impoverished for a variety of reasons, it is clear from the legislative scheme that the payments are designed to provide income assistance. In the instant case, the plaintiff respondent required income assistance over many years because she had suffered psychological injury as a result of abuse and was rendered less capable of obtaining employment and earning income as a result. There is no question but that she received benefits as "income replacement." As I have noted, she claimed in this action that she was, because of the tort, less able to earn income by reasons of her injuries. She claimed for past and future loss of income. The trial judge made awards under those heads of damages.
[144] In my judgment, the social assistance payments the respondent received were a partial replacement of her income loss, or her capacity to earn income. These payments received by her do not fall within the insurance or pension exceptions. Nor in my view, do they have the character of charitable payments. This was not a situation similar to that in Redpath, supra, where a subscription was organized for the victims of a misfortune. Rather, it is a situation where payments were made to the respondent pursuant to a statutory income assistance scheme. I am in agreement with Mackenzie J.A. that these payments should not be categorized as within the charitable payments exception.
Therefore, in my judgment, the trial judge did not err in making the deduction she did from the past loss of income award. It follows that I would not accede to the respondent's argument that we ought to overrule M.(M.) v. F.(R.), referred to supra. In my view, that case was correctly decided.

[148] Further, I agree with Mr. Justice Mackenzie and with Mr. Justice Hall that income assistance payments do not fall within the private insurance exception. In Cunningham v. Wheeler, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 359, Cory J., speaking for the majority, founded this exception on the fairness inherent in allowing the plaintiff to keep what he has earned. At para. 82, he said:
I think the exemption for the private policy of insurance should be maintained. It has a long history. It is understood and accepted. There has never been any confusion as to when it should be applied. More importantly it is based on fairness. All who insure themselves for disability benefits are displaying wisdom and forethought in making provision for the continuation of some income in case of disabling injury or illness. The acquisition of the policy has social benefits for those insured, their dependants and indeed their community. It represents forbearance and self-denial on the part of the purchaser of the policy to provide for contingencies. The individual may never make a claim on the policy and the premiums paid may be a total loss. Yet the policy provides security. (my emphasis)
Cory J. acknowledged fairness and justice as the reason for the exception in his dissenting reasons in Ratych v. Bloomer, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 940, as well, at 950. Income assistance payments do not fit this mould. They involve no element of individual forbearance, self-denial, or forethought by recipients - they are funded by the taxpayers generally and anyone who satisfies the qualifying criteria is entitled to receive them.

whether the plaintiff has suffered a loss that the defendant is legally obliged to offset. As McLachlin J. (now C.J.C.) said, in her majority judgment in Ratych v. Bloomer, at p. 964:
I conclude that the general principles underlying our system of tort law suggest that the damages awarded to the plaintiff should be confined to his or her actual loss, as closely as that can be calculated. The damages should be in an amount which will restore the plaintiff to his pre-accident position. Where pecuniary losses, such as loss of earnings, are at stake, the measure of damages is normally the plaintiff's actual financial loss. Unless the plaintiff can demonstrate such loss, he or she is not entitled to recover. As Lord Diplock stated in Browning v. War Office, [1962] 3 All E.R. 1089, at pp. 1094-95: "A person who acts without reasonable care does no wrong in law; he commits no tort. He only does wrong, he only commits a tort, if his lack of care causes damage to the plaintiff."
[152] Of course, if the collateral payer is entitled to be subrogated to the plaintiff's claim, the collateral payments cannot offset the plaintiff's loss. The right to subrogation is normally created by contract, as in the case of private insurance, or by statute, as in the case of some statutory benefits. Subrogation may also be achieved by the courts through the imposition of a trust upon an award or by a direction to pay in favour of persons in close relationship to the plaintiff who have gratuitously provided necessary services, such as nursing care: see Ratych v. Bloomer, supra, at 978-79. As McLachlin J. said at 979, the justification for such court-imposed subrogation:
... may be seen as a moral obligation on the part of the injured plaintiff to repay those who rendered services to him gratuitously, coupled with the desirability of avoiding the injustice which would result from the inability to otherwise compensate the persons who rendered services, given that they had no independent cause of action.
[153] In such cases, the loss caused by the tort has been conditionally absorbed by the collateral payer and restitution of the payer's loss is accomplished derivatively through the plaintiff's claim against the tortfeasor. Thus, it is not the plaintiff's loss at all. If the plaintiff does not recover from the tortfeasor, the collateral payer suffers the loss. If the plaintiff does recover, the payer's loss is recompensed by the tortfeasor.
[154] When subrogation is not a relevant consideration, it must be determined whether the collateral payments were received on account of the plaintiff's loss. To the extent that they were so received, the plaintiff's loss has been recompensed and the tortfeasor cannot be called upon to pay.
[155] The relevant pre-trial damage alleged by the plaintiff in her statement of claim in this case was "a loss of income." Although, the trial judge characterized the claim as one for "loss of earning capacity", it is my view that the effect of her award was to replace a lost income stream. The trial judge implicitly recognized this as the essence of the award when she based it upon statistical evidence of average employment earnings of females resident in British Columbia (see her reasons at [2000] B.C.J. No. 909 (Q.L.), para. 310). Moreover, this view is consistent with fundamental principle. The measure of damages is the plaintiff's actual financial loss, not the theoretical value of an untapped abstract capacity to earn.
In my view, the difference in phraseology in respect of pre-trial loss between "loss of income" and "loss of earning capacity" is terminological, not substantive.
[156] Consequently, the award of damages for pre-trial loss of income in this case has converted a past uncertainty into a certainty - but for her tortiously-caused injuries, the plaintiff would have been employed during the pre-trial period and would have earned income from her employment.
[157] The corollary of this conclusion is that the plaintiff would not have received income assistance benefits while she was working. It is implicit in the deduction of the income assistance payments by the trial judge that, as a matter of fact, the plaintiff would not have been eligible to receive them while she was gainfully employed. It follows that the income assistance payments that the plaintiff received had the effect of partially replacing her lost employment income.

In Ratych v. Bloomer, supra, at 972, McLachlin J. referred to Lord Reid's comment in Parry v. Cleaver, [1969] 1 All E.R. 555 (H.L.) at 560 to the effect that wages paid to a person while he is off work do not differ in kind from the wages paid while he is working, with the result that we never reach the question of how we treat sums he never would have received but for the accident. As I understand her reasons, McLachlin J. accepted that proposition when she rejected the argument that the court must assume that a quid pro quo was paid by the plaintiff for the wages received while he was off work and when she reiterated, at 973, that "a plaintiff is obliged to prove his or her loss."
[161] The comments of both learned jurists were made in the context of a consideration of payments received as a result of an employer-employee relationship, but this relationship is not the critical element of their analyses. Rather, it is the nature of the payments that is important. In both cases the payments were qualitatively equivalent to wages received in consideration for the plaintiff's work. Substituting "income" for "wages" in Lord Reid's dictum, it is my view that to the extent that a plaintiff receives income while he is off work that does not differ in kind from the income that he receives while he is working, he has suffered no loss of income.

I can find nothing in either Ratych or Cunningham which purports to overrule Boarelli insofar as it relates to the non-deductibility of welfare benefits. The deductibility of those benefits was not in issue in either of the Supreme Court of Canada decisions.
It is fair to say, however, that, in Ratych, Madam Justice McLachlin disapproved of Boarelli insofar as it pronounced on the deductibility of a broad range of other collateral benefits. In her view, Boarelli adopted a far too expansive view of the non-deductibility of other benefits

Unless the social assistance benefits duplicate damages under a particular head of damage in the tort award, it cannot be said that retention of them would result in double recovery. Thus, in this case, unless the social assistance benefits are a form of wage or earnings replacement, then it cannot be said that M.B. has been overcompensated by being paid twice for the same loss.
It does not appear that this argument was made in either M.(M.) or Jones, which apparently proceeded on the assumption that receipt of social assistance payments resulted in double recovery for past wage loss, the only question being whether these payments fell within one of the exceptions to the rule against double recovery.
[50] As earlier noted, the English Court of Appeal in Lincoln, and the House of Lords in Hodgson v. Trapp, regarded the receipt of social assistance benefits in addition to a tort award as a form of double recovery which could not be justified. This view was shared by the U.K. Parliament which subsequently enacted legislation to deal directly with this issue. But the legislation in England bears no resemblance to that in place in British Columbia pursuant to which the payments to M.B. were made. With due respect to the views of Lord Bridge in Hodgson to the contrary, I consider it essential to have regard to the nature and purpose of the legislation under which these benefits were paid in determining whether the issue of double recovery arises.
[51] Of the approximately $122,000 in social assistance payments made to M.B. prior to trial, approximately $100,000 was paid pursuant to the Guaranteed Available Income For Need Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 158, (the "GAIN Act") and Regulations thereto. The balance was paid under the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act and the Income Assistance Regulation, B.C. Reg. 75/97. The latter Act, which came into effect on July 30, 1996, was considered by Mr. Justice Donald in M.(M.).
[52] In general terms, the purpose of the GAIN Act was to provide income assistance to those in need. "Income assistance" was defined in s. 1 to mean:
(a) financial assistance; . . . or (f) generally any other form of aid
that is necessary for the purpose of relieving poverty, neglect or suffering; . . .
[53] In addition to financial assistance, the Act also provided for other kinds of assistance for individuals in need, including health care, day care, and homemaker services, and retraining, rehabilitation and other employment-enhancement services.
[54] The GAIN Act specifically provided for the assignment of maintenance rights to the Crown by individuals in receipt of social assistance. That was the only form of assignment of rights referred to in the Act. The only provision in the Act for recovery of "overpayment[s]" of benefits related to situations involving non-disclosure, fraud, error or other causes whereby an individual received benefits to which he was not entitled. There was no provision in the Act for repayment of benefits provided to individuals who subsequently recovered damages in tort.
[55] Section 26(2) of the Act provided that the Lieutenant Governor in Council may make regulations, including regulations:
(c) defining individuals or classes of individuals who qualify for classes of income assistance or social services; (d) prescribing rules for eligibility of individuals or classes of individuals for income assistance or social services; (e) prescribing rules for determining the rate or amount of income assistance and social services;
[56] The Regulations enacted pursuant to s. 26 of the Act (B.C. Reg. 479/76, in effect as of 1976) provided, amongst other things, that "'Benefits' mean income assistance or social services provided under the Act and these regulations." The Regulations defined "earned" and "unearned" income which included both moneys and other benefits. Section 8 of the Regulations provided for circumstances in which "there is no eligibility for income assistance", most of which were related to the applicant's level of income. Section 10 of the Regulations set forth the basis for entitlement to benefits under the Act:
10. Within the limits of the Act and these regulations, an individual eligible for income assistance shall be entitled to receive for himself or herself, and any dependants, income assistance not exceeding the difference between the prescribed amount of benefits set in Schedule A of these regulations and the amount of any nonexempt income available to the applicant and any dependants as prescribed in Schedule B of these regulations.
Schedule A set out basic income assistance rates.
[57] The Regulations went on to provide for other benefits and services available to applicants including: "provision for educational or rehabilitation services"; "burial or cremation of deceased individuals"; "provisions for individuals requiring special care"; "special services to children"; "homemaker-housekeeper services"; "day care services", "healthcare services"; and "pharmacare".
[58] In my view, there is nothing in the GAIN Act or Regulations which supports the proposition that social assistance benefits were a form of wage replacement or were intended to be compensatory. The benefits provided took the form of both money and services. The essential qualification for obtaining benefits was need. "Income assistance" was defined as meaning assistance through money and services "that is necessary for the purpose of relieving poverty, neglect or suffering." Past employment was not a requirement for benefits and some who received benefits, including persons with physical and mental disabilities, were permanently unemployable. The benefits were not stated to be a form of wage replacement but simply "income assistance".
[59] To the extent that the Legislature turned its mind to ensuring that recipients were not overpaid, it did so in limited circumstances. If overpayment occurred because of fraud, error or other cause going to the initial entitlement to benefits, then benefits must be repaid. If a person had a right to maintenance payments, then the Crown could seek an assignment of those benefits to ensure that the qualifying recipient was paid, but not overpaid.
[60] Does an analysis of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act or Regulations lead to a different conclusion? In my view, it does not. The two pieces of legislation are similar in purpose and intent, although the latter Act may be viewed as placing more emphasis on programs leading to self-sufficiency than the former. A similar conclusion was reached by Madam Justice Baker in Grace v. British Columbia (Lieutenant-Governor in Council), [2000] B.C.J. No. 1201 (B.C.S.C.) (Q.L.), as reflected by the following passages at paras. 80 and 82 of that decision:
I do not agree that the intent of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act is fundamentally different from the intent of its predecessor [the GAIN Act]. . . . The present (Income Assistance) Act may place more emphasis on the relief of poverty through assisting individuals to become self-sufficient, but the purpose of the legislation remains the same - the provision of income support and social services to residents of British Columbia who are in need and the relief of poverty, neglect and suffering in a financially accountable and administratively efficient manner within the limits of the budget set for the Ministry from time to time.
[61] Mr. Justice Donald reviewed the provisions of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act in M.(M.). I do not find it useful to repeat his analysis in that regard. In essence, the range of benefits provided under the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act to individuals and families include the same types of benefits provided under the GAIN Act and Regulations.
[62] Mr. Justice Donald's conclusions with respect to the nature and purpose of the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act are set forth at para. 45 of these reasons. In coming to those conclusions, he was considering the receipt of these benefits within the context of the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. While I am considering a different question, namely, whether the receipt of these benefits results in double recovery, I agree with his conclusions with respect to the nature and purpose of the Act.
[63] In my view, a reasonable conclusion one can draw from Mr. Justice Donald's analysis in M.(M.), and from the Acts and Regulations pursuant to which these benefits were paid, is that social assistance benefits do not give rise to double recovery because they are not in the nature of wage replacement. Entitlement to the benefits payable under either the GAIN Act or the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act is in no way related to, or dependant upon, the claimant having suffered a loss caused by a tort. Payment of social assistance benefits is not synonymous with, or even roughly correlative to, payments for past wage loss.
To view them in that way is simply to impose a tort-damages analysis on payments which were not designed to, and do not, duplicate payments by tortfeasors to victims of torts.
[64] Applicants for social assistance benefits may well be victims of torts and their need may be related to the fact that a tort has been committed against them. But the Acts pursuant to which these benefits were paid do not purport to deal with, or contemplate, repayment of benefits from the proceeds of tort awards. Nor do they provide for an assignment of any portion of a tort award for damages. In that regard, it is interesting to note that the B.C. Benefits Manual relating to the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act, provides (under the heading "Policy") that "Assignment or repayment agreements are NOT to be completed for recipients pending ICBC settlements." No reason for this policy is provided, nor were counsel able to assist in that regard.
[65] If the Legislature had intended to do away with a tort victim's rights to collateral benefits, it could readily have done so in a variety of ways. The issue of double recovery in tort has been around for a long time. The Legislature must be taken to be aware of the issue. Decisions such as Parry v. Cleaver, Boarelli and Cunningham have emphasized that, if the retention of benefits in addition to damage awards gives rise to a significant problem, the Legislature is in the best position to weigh the competing social interests and intervene.
Providing rights of subrogation to the payor, an assignment of benefits by a payee, or the imposition of a trust in favour of the payor of benefits provided to the payee are possible alternatives for dealing with this issue if legislation is considered appropriate.
[66] In the result, I am not persuaded that the benefits received by M.B. under either the GAIN Act or the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act duplicate the damage award she received for past loss of earning capacity. When one looks at the nature and purpose of these statutes, it is apparent that the benefits paid pursuant to them constitute income assistance, but not wage replacement. They were paid to her for the same reason they are paid to any recipient, "for the purpose of relieving poverty, neglect or suffering." They were payable as a matter of statutory entitlement independent of any right she may have had to recover damages

Courts now ask whether the payments under consideration are compensatory payments, similar to and directed at the same head of loss as the potential award. They now tend to focus on the question of possible "double recovery." For instance, in Cunningham v. Wheeler, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 359 at 396, Cory J. observed the following concerning the leading principle of recovery of damages in tort cases:
At the outset, it may be well to state once again the principle of recovery in an action for tort. Simply, it is to compensate the injured party as completely as possible for the loss suffered as a result of the negligent action or inaction of the defendant. However, the plaintiff is not entitled to a double recovery for any loss arising from the injury.
[136] That is, of course, not an entirely new principle. An often quoted early authority on the subject may be found in Livingstone v. The Rawyards Coal Company, [1880] 5 A.C. 25, a case involving trespass to land. There, Lord Blackburn stated as follows at p. 39:
I do not think there is any difference of opinion as to its being a general rule that, where any injury is to be compensated by damages, in settling the sum of money to be given for reparation of damages you should as nearly as possible get at that sum of money which will put the party who has been injured, or who has suffered, in the same position as he would have been in if he had not sustained the wrong for which he is now getting his compensation or reparation.

the payments are designed to provide income assistance. In the instant case, the plaintiff respondent required income assistance over many years because she had suffered psychological injury as a result of abuse and was rendered less capable of obtaining employment and earning income as a result. There is no question but that she received benefits as "income replacement." As I have noted, she claimed in this action that she was, because of the tort, less able to earn income by reasons of her injuries. She claimed for past and future loss of income. The trial judge made awards under those heads of damages.
[144] In my judgment, the social assistance payments the respondent received were a partial replacement of her income loss, or her capacity to earn income. These payments received by her do not fall within the insurance or pension exceptions. Nor in my view, do they have the character of charitable payments. This was not a situation similar to that in Redpath, supra, where a subscription was organized for the victims of a misfortune. Rather, it is a situation where payments were made to the respondent pursuant to a statutory income assistance scheme. I am in agreement with Mackenzie J.A. that these payments should not be categorized as within the charitable payments exception.
Therefore, in my judgment, the trial judge did not err in making the deduction she did from the past loss of income award. It follows that I would not accede to the respondent's argument that we ought to overrule M.(M.) v. F.(R.), referred to supra. In my view, that case was correctly decided.

[148] Further, I agree with Mr. Justice Mackenzie and with Mr. Justice Hall that income assistance payments do not fall within the private insurance exception. In Cunningham v. Wheeler, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 359, Cory J., speaking for the majority, founded this exception on the fairness inherent in allowing the plaintiff to keep what he has earned. At para. 82, he said:
I think the exemption for the private policy of insurance should be maintained. It has a long history. It is understood and accepted. There has never been any confusion as to when it should be applied. More importantly it is based on fairness. All who insure themselves for disability benefits are displaying wisdom and forethought in making provision for the continuation of some income in case of disabling injury or illness. The acquisition of the policy has social benefits for those insured, their dependants and indeed their community. It represents forbearance and self-denial on the part of the purchaser of the policy to provide for contingencies. The individual may never make a claim on the policy and the premiums paid may be a total loss. Yet the policy provides security. (my emphasis)

Income assistance payments do not fit this mould. They involve no element of individual forbearance, self-denial, or forethought by recipients - they are funded by the taxpayers generally and anyone who satisfies the qualifying criteria is entitled to receive them.
[149] Further, I agree with Mr. Justice Hall that M.(M.) v. F.(R.) (1997), 52 B.C.L.R. (3d) 127 (C.A.) was correctly decided. In my opinion, the effect of Ratych v. Bloomer, supra, and of Cunningham v. Wheeler, supra, is that all collateral payments in the nature of income that have been received by a plaintiff must be taken into account in an award of damages for past loss of income unless they fall within the private insurance or charitable exceptions.
[150] I agree, as well, with Mr. Justice Hall that the plaintiff in this case cannot keep both

whether the plaintiff has suffered a loss that the defendant is legally obliged to offset. As McLachlin J. (now C.J.C.) said, in her majority judgment in Ratych v. Bloomer, at p. 964:
I conclude that the general principles underlying our system of tort law suggest that the damages awarded to the plaintiff should be confined to his or her actual loss, as closely as that can be calculated. The damages should be in an amount which will restore the plaintiff to his pre-accident position. Where pecuniary losses, such as loss of earnings, are at stake, the measure of damages is normally the plaintiff's actual financial loss. Unless the plaintiff can demonstrate such loss, he or she is not entitled to recover. As Lord Diplock stated in Browning v. War Office, [1962] 3 All E.R. 1089, at pp. 1094-95: "A person who acts without reasonable care does no wrong in law; he commits no tort. He only does wrong, he only commits a tort, if his lack of care causes damage to the plaintiff."
[152] Of course, if the collateral payer is entitled to be subrogated to the plaintiff's claim, the collateral payments cannot offset the plaintiff's loss. The right to subrogation is normally created by contract, as in the case of private insurance, or by statute, as in the case of some statutory benefits. Subrogation may also be achieved by the courts through the imposition of a trust upon an award or by a direction to pay in favour of persons in close relationship to the plaintiff who have gratuitously provided necessary services, such as nursing care: see Ratych v. Bloomer, supra, at 978-79. As McLachlin J. said at 979, the justification for such court-imposed subrogation:
... may be seen as a moral obligation on the part of the injured plaintiff to repay those who rendered services to him gratuitously, coupled with the desirability of avoiding the injustice which would result from the inability to otherwise compensate the persons who rendered services, given that they had no independent cause of action.
[153] In such cases, the loss caused by the tort has been conditionally absorbed by the collateral payer and restitution of the payer's loss is accomplished derivatively through the plaintiff's claim against the tortfeasor. Thus, it is not the plaintiff's loss at all. If the plaintiff does not recover from the tortfeasor, the collateral payer suffers the loss. If the plaintiff does recover, the payer's loss is recompensed by the tortfeasor.
[154] When subrogation is not a relevant consideration, it must be determined whether the collateral payments were received on account of the plaintiff's loss. To the extent that they were so received, the plaintiff's loss has been recompensed and the tortfeasor cannot be called upon to pay.
[155] The relevant pre-trial damage alleged by the plaintiff in her statement of claim in this case was "a loss of income." Although, the trial judge characterized the claim as one for "loss of earning capacity", it is my view that the effect of her award was to replace a lost income stream. The trial judge implicitly recognized this as the essence of the award when she based it upon statistical evidence of average employment earnings of females resident in British Columbia (see her reasons at [2000] B.C.J. No. 909 (Q.L.), para. 310). Moreover, this view is consistent with fundamental principle. The measure of damages is the plaintiff's actual financial loss, not the theoretical value of an untapped abstract capacity to earn.
In my view, the difference in phraseology in respect of pre-trial loss between "loss of income" and "loss of earning capacity" is terminological, not substantive.
[156] Consequently, the award of damages for pre-trial loss of income in this case has converted a past uncertainty into a certainty - but for her tortiously-caused injuries, the plaintiff would have been employed during the pre-trial period and would have earned income from her employment.
[157] The corollary of this conclusion is that the plaintiff would not have received income assistance benefits while she was working. It is implicit in the deduction of the income assistance payments by the trial judge that, as a matter of fact, the plaintiff would not have been eligible to receive them while she was gainfully employed. It follows that the income assistance payments that the plaintiff received had the effect of partially replacing her lost employment income.

supporting_passages.text:
The courts, however, have consistently recognized and affirmed two exceptions to the rule against double recovery: the private insurance exception and the charitable or benevolent gifts exception. Since both of those exceptions are relied upon by counsel for M.B. as alternative bases for justifying the retention of social assistance benefits by M.B., I will refer to them at some length.
(a) The Private Insurance Exception
[21] The history of the private insurance exception to the rule against double recovery was canvassed by both Mr. Justice Cory and Madam Justice McLachlin (as she then was), speaking for the majority and the minority, respectively, in Cunningham, supra. There, Mr. Justice Cory noted that the private insurance exception to the rule against double recovery, whereby payments made pursuant to a private policy of insurance for loss of wages are not deducted from the lost wages claim of a plaintiff, had been the law in Canada and in England for well over a century. He observed that the rule had its genesis in the decision of Bradburn v. Great Western Rail Co., [1874-80] All E.R. Rep. 195 (Ex.
Div.), in which the original justification for the exception was set forth in the reasons of Pigott B., at p. 197 of that decision:
. . . I think that there would be no justice or principle in setting off an amount which the plaintiff has entitled himself to under a contract of insurance, such as any prudent man would make on the principle of, as the expression is, "laying by for a rainy day." He pays the premiums upon a contract which, if he meets with an accident, entitles him to receive a sum of money. It is not because he meets with the accident, but because he made a contract with, and paid premiums to, the insurance company, for that express purpose, that he gets the money from them. It is true that there must be the element of accident in order to entitle him to the money; but it is under and by reason of his contract with the insurance company, that he gets the amount;
and I think that it ought not, upon any principle of justice, to be deducted from the amount of the damages proved to have been sustained by him through the negligence of the defendants. [22] Mr. Justice Cory noted that the basis for the private insurance exception later shifted from the primarily causal analysis set out in Bradburn, to the rationale that where the plaintiff had demonstrated forethought and prudence in obtaining insurance, the benefit should enure to the plaintiff and not the defendant. This reasoning was adopted by the House of Lords in Parry v. Cleaver, [1969] 1 All E.R. 555, and was referred to by Mr. Justice Cory as a justification for the exception on the basis of fairness. At para.
82 of the Cunningham decision, after noting that Bradburn had been consistently applied by Canadian courts, Mr. Justice Cory stated:
I think the exemption for the private policy of insurance should be maintained. It has a long history. It is understood and accepted. There has never been any confusion as to when it should be applied. More importantly it is based on fairness. All who insure themselves for disability benefits are displaying wisdom and forethought in making provision for the continuation of some income in case of disabling injury or illness. The acquisition of the policy has social benefits for those insured, their dependants and indeed their community. It represents forebearance and self-denial on the part of the purchaser of the policy to provide for contingencies. The individual may never make a claim on the policy and the premiums paid may be a total loss. Yet the policy provides security.
[23] Cory J. went on to add that he could see no reason why a tortfeasor should benefit from the sacrifices made by a plaintiff in obtaining an insurance policy to provide for lost wages. Further, in his view, the private insurance exception should be extended to include insurance benefits flowing from a collective agreement. At paras. 88 and 89 of the decision, Cory J. stated:
To say that the exception applies only to private insurance, where actual premiums are paid to the insurance company, would create barriers that are unfair and artificial. It would mean that top management and professionals who could well afford to purchase their own insurance would have the benefit of the insurance exception, while those who made the same provision and made relatively greater financial sacrifices to provide for the disability payments through their collective bargaining agreement would be denied the benefits of the insurance exception. This would be manifestly unfair. There is no basis for such a socially regressive distinction. Union representation and collective bargaining are recognized as a means for working people to protect their interests.
The benefits for which employees have bargained in good faith should not be sacrificed simply because the mode of payment for the disability payments is different from that in private insurance contracts. Where evidence is adduced that an employee-plaintiff has paid in some manner for his or her benefits under a collective agreement or contract of employment, the insurance exception should apply. It would be unjust to deprive employees of the benefits which, through prudence and thrift, they have provided for themselves.
[24] Madam Justice McLachlin, speaking for the minority in Cunningham, agreed that the private insurance exception to double recovery should continue to be recognized. In her view, however, that exception should be confined to situations where there was evidence that the plaintiff had contributed to the insurance scheme from which he or she benefited. She did not regard it as sufficient for the plaintiff to assert that there was a contribution by virtue of the plaintiff being the beneficiary of a collective agreement negotiated with the employer on behalf of all employees. She clearly favoured restricting the private insurance exception within narrow limits, rather than expanding it to fit a broader spectrum of plaintiffs.
This accorded with her analysis of the law in England which was moving toward general deductibility of almost all collateral benefits, primarily through legislative reform. It also accorded with the views of many academics writing in the area of damages, who almost universally favour a strict rule of deductibility of collateral benefits including, in some cases, collateral benefits provided for by private insurance funded by the plaintiff.
[25] In the result, I have concluded that it is unnecessary to resolve the question of whether the social assistance benefits received by M.B. can be brought within the private insurance exception to the double recovery rule. It is clear, however, that the law in Canada not only recognizes the private insurance exception to the rule against double recovery, but it has taken an expansive interpretation of that exception.
(b) The Charitable Gifts Exception [26] The charitable gifts exception to the double recovery rule is also discussed in Cunningham. Although that exception was not in issue in those proceedings, there was no dispute that the charitable gifts exception was well established in English and Canadian law and that it should be retained. Madam Justice McLachlin discussed the charitable gifts exception at p. 370 of her reasons:
The first exception to the rule against double recovery is the case of charitable gifts. If a plaintiff is injured and his neighbour brings him a basket of groceries or donates to him a sum of money, the law will not deduct the value of the basket from the damages which the negligent defendant must pay nor require that the monetary gift be called into account. This exception reflects the concern of the courts who initiated it that people should not be discouraged from aiding those in misfortune. Arguably, it also reflects the reality that in most cases it would be more trouble than it is worth to require the courts to hear evidence and rule on the value of charitable assistance.
[27] This exception has also been held to apply to disaster funds set up for victims, including victims of torts, for the purpose of alleviating their losses. The leading case in that regard is Redpath v. Belfast and County Down Railway, [1947] N.I. 167 (K.B.), where such a fund was contributed to by members of the public to assist the victims of a train accident caused by the negligence of the servants of the defendant railway. The proceedings came before the court on a motion by the defendants to compel the plaintiff to answer questions about moneys he had received from the disaster fund, with a view to having them taken into account in the assessment of damages.
The defendant submitted that the moneys received should be set off against the plaintiff's claim for damages for past wage loss. The plaintiff opposed the motion on the basis that the information sought was irrelevant to the issue of damages. The court agreed with the plaintiff and dismissed the defendant's motion.
[28] Andrews L.C.J. noted that there was no evidence that the moneys paid from the disaster fund were directed toward any particular head of damage and, further, that if the defendants should succeed in their motion, the likely effect would be "that the springs of private charity would be found to be largely, if not entirely, dried up." After reviewing various authorities, he concluded as follows, at p. 175 of the decision:
In these circumstances common sense and natural justice appear to me to rise in revolt against the proposition that the money so subscribed should be diverted from the objects whom the subscribers intended to benefit in order to be applied in reduction of the damages properly payable by the wrongdoer as compensation to the victims for their loss. Why, one may well ask, should the defendants' burden be lightened by the generosity of the public?
It is for the party who is in default to pay for such damage as he has caused and which is directly occasioned by his negligence without bringing into the account in reduction of his liability any moneys which may be received by the injured party without legal right from a fund voluntarily subscribed from charitable motives by third parties after the damage had accrued. The possibility of such a fund being formed is a contingency altogether too remote to enter into the calculation and assessment of damages. The creation of the fund was a circumstance of a wholly independent or collateral character to the defendants' negligence. . . .
Thus, the decision that these moneys should not be taken into account relied on principles of remoteness, public policy and fairness.
[29] The case most frequently cited in discussing the charitable gifts exception to the double recovery rule is Parry v. Cleaver, supra, particularly the judgment of Lord Reid. At p. 14 of the decision, Lord Reid stated:
. . . I take first the case of benevolence. I do not use the word "charity" because, rightly or wrongly, many people object to it. I know of no better statement of the reason [for this exception] than that of Andrews C.J. in Redpath v. Belfast and County Down Railway [citation and quotation omitted]. It would be revolting to the ordinary man's sense of justice, and therefore contrary to public policy, that the sufferer should have his damages reduced so that he would gain nothing from the benevolence of his friends or relations or of the public at large, and that the only gainer would be the wrongdoer.
We do not have to decide in this case whether these considerations also apply to public benevolence in the shape of various uncovenanted benefits from the welfare state, but it may be thought that Parliament did not intend them to be for the benefit of the wrongdoer.

In the event I am in error in finding that the receipt of social assistance benefits by M.B. did not result in her obtaining double recovery under her claim for past loss of earning capacity, I propose to deal with the other submissions before the Court. These submissions are founded on the assumption that double recovery would result if M.B. were to retain the social assistance benefits and the full amount of her tort damages for past loss of earning capacity.
(6) Applicability of the "Charitable Gifts" Exception
[72] The nature of this exception to the rule against double recovery and the principal authorities in relation to it are discussed at paras. 26-48, supra.
[73] The Boarelli decision is clear authority for the proposition that social assistance benefits are not deductible from an award of damages on the basis of the "charitable gifts" exception to the rule against double recovery. In M.(M.), however, a majority of this Court, Mr. Justice Donald dissenting, found that Boarelli had been overruled in its entirety by the majority decision in Ratych.
[74] As I stated at para. 36 of these reasons, I am unable to find anything in the Ratych decision which purports to overrule Boarelli insofar as that decision discusses the deductibility of welfare benefits. The criticism of Boarelli by Madam Justice McLachlin for the majority in Ratych, was that, despite the fact that the only issue before the Court of Appeal in Boarelli was the deductibility of welfare benefits, "the Court took it upon itself to pronounce on a wide variety of other benefits", and took a broad non-deductibility approach to those benefits.
While the majority in Ratych disapproved of this broad-based approach to the deductibility of collateral benefits, it did not purport to pronounce on that aspect of the Boarelli judgment dealing with the deductibility of welfare benefits. It neither approved, nor disapproved, the deductibility of those benefits. Rather, Madam Justice McLachlin made a point of stating, at p. 983 of the Ratych decision, that her comments on the deductibility of wage benefits "should not be taken as extending to types of collateral benefits other than lost earnings, such as insurance paid for by the plaintiff and gratuitous payments made by third parties." She specifically left those matters, which were not before the court, for another day.
[75] Certainly, there is nothing in the Cunningham decision which comments adversely on the Boarelli decision. On the contrary, Boarelli was cited by Mr. Justice Cory as an application of the Bradburn decision with respect to the private insurance exception to the rule against double recovery.
[76] In addition to finding that Boarelli had been overruled by the Supreme Court of Canada, the majority in M.(M.) rejected the submission that social assistance benefits fell within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. They did so for two reasons. First, the exception, as described by Madam Justice McLachlin in Cunningham, was framed as being in relation to charitable gifts made by "people", that is, individuals. The objection to deductibility in Cunningham was said to be based on the concern that individuals may be deterred from making such gifts if they were aware that they would be deducted from an award of damages, and thereby enure to the benefit of the tortfeasor.
Secondly, the concern was expressed that there may be difficulties in assessing the value of charitable gifts such that it was not worth the effort to deduct them. The majority in M.(M.) found that neither of these justifications for non-deductibility applied to social assistance benefits provided by the state.
[77] As earlier stated, I agree with Mr. Justice Donald in M.(M.) that the nature and purpose of social assistance benefits are fundamentally charitable in that they are designed to provide assistance to those in need, however that need arises. In the case of social assistance benefits, however, the source of benevolence is not individuals, but the state. The state, in turn, funds this benevolence through the tax-paying public.
[78] It is true that the provision of social assistance benefits to victims of torts differs from the provision of a basket of groceries by a neighbour, or from the provision of disaster relief funds, in that the victim has no legal entitlement to the groceries or to moneys from the fund, whereas the victim of a tort may be entitled to social assistance if the financial and other legislative criteria are met. (As Mackenzie J.A. observes in his reasons for judgment, the concept of entitlement is reinforced by reference to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, U.N. Doc. A/810 (1948) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights 1966, U.N. Doc.
A/6316, Articles 9 and 11.) I note, however, that the entitlement to social assistance benefits is founded primarily on poverty, or need, the same foundation as for other charitable gifts. In that regard, I would reiterate the following passage from the judgment of Mr. Justice Donald in M.(M.), in which he discusses the nature of the provision of social assistance benefits under the B.C. Benefits (Income Assistance) Act (at para. 85):
The [social assistance] scheme is society's collective response to the needs of the poor, a task once undertaken by religious institutions but now thought to be more effectively discharged by a public agency with a stable funding base provided by all taxpayers. The scheme arises from the notion that we are our brothers' keepers and that we must show compassion for the poor. In that sense the scheme is undoubtedly charitable in nature and clearly falls within the recognized exception in Boarelli.
[79] I recognize that the aspect of entitlement to these benefits distinguishes them from traditional concepts of charity to the extent that they cannot be said to fall directly within the charitable gifts exception to the rule against double recovery. In my view, however, they are sufficiently analogous to charity in all other respects that they can be reasonably brought under the umbrella of this exception.
[80] In answer to the view of the majority in M.(M.) that, unlike valuing other charitable gifts, valuing social assistance benefits does not present a problem, I agree with Mr. Justice Donald that social assistance benefits are myriad in form and that, if the value of all benefits were to be taken into account and deducted from a tort award, the task would be daunting.
